108 Finger Permutations - Level 2
Two-String Transfer: 2+2 Adjacent-String Coordination
This level keeps the same 108 finger codes and fifth-position fret map, but moves every four-note cell across two strings.
1. Same left-hand language
1 = index / fret 5
2 = middle / fret 6
3 = ring / fret 7
4 = pinky / fret 8
No position shift is added yet.
2. New movement rule
Notes 1-2: first string of the pair
Notes 3-4: adjacent second string
Walk E/A, A/D, D/G, G/B, B/e,
then return e/B through A/E.
3. Practice one set at a time
Each set contains 12 exercises.
Run once starting with a downstroke.
Run again starting with an upstroke.
Rotate your existing rhythm groupings.
Do not run all 108 in one session.
Worked example - code 1234
The digits stay in the order 1-2-3-4. Only the strings carrying them change.
ASCEND

B|--------|--------|--------|----7-8-|5-6-----|
G|--------|--------|----7-8-|5-6-----|--------|
D|--------|----7-8-|5-6-----|--------|--------|
A|----7-8-|5-6-----|--------|--------|--------|
E|5-6-----|--------|--------|--------|--------|
DESCEND
e|5-6-----|--------|--------|--------|--------|
B|----7-8-|5-6-----|--------|--------|--------|
G|--------|----7-8-|5-6-----|--------|--------|
D|--------|--------|----7-8-|5-6-----|--------|
A|--------|--------|--------|----7-8-|5-6-----|
E|--------|--------|--------|--------|----7-8-|
Progression rule
1
Choose one 12-exercise set.
2
Use one rhythmic grouping for that session.
3
Play every exercise up and down continuously.
4
Repeat with the opposite starting pick stroke.
5
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next time.
6
After two errors or rising tension,
reduce 4-6 BPM.
Advance when a full set is clean in both pick-start directions on two separate days.
Standard tuning. Fifth position. Keep the code order intact on both ascent and descent.
Page 1 of 10

lines.text: For every adjacent string pair, play digits 1-2 of the code on the first string and digits 3-4 on the second string.

108 Finger Permutations - Level 3
Odd-Count String Transfer: 3+1 / 1+3 Split-Point Control
Level 2 crossed after note 2. Level 3 moves the crossing to an odd beat, changing the inside/outside geometry of alternate picking.
1. Keep the foundation fixed
1 = index / fret 5
2 = middle / fret 6
3 = ring / fret 7
4 = pinky / fret 8
No position shift or string skip yet.
2. Move the crossing point
Mode A, 3+1: cross after note 3.
Mode B, 1+3: cross after note 1.
Run the same adjacent pairs up and down.
The four-digit code never changes.
3. Separate before combining
Use one 12-code set and one mode per session.
Repeat with downstroke and upstroke starts.
Combine the modes only after each is clean.
Even tone matters more than top speed.

3+1: notes 1-2-3 on the first string; note 4 on the adjacent string.

SECOND PASS
Remove the accent and make all four notes equal in volume.

SECOND PASS
Remove the accent and make all four notes equal in volume.
Every exercise page includes both ascending and descending adjacent-pair routes.
Session protocol
1
Begin 8-12 BPM below your clean Level 2 tempo.
2
Session A: one 12-code set in Mode A. Session B: the same set in Mode B.
3
Play each exercise up and down, first with a downstroke start and then with an upstroke start.

After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next time. After two errors or
rising tension, reduce 4-6 BPM.
5
Advance when both mode pages are clean on two separate days; then
try alternating 3+1 and 1+3 between successive string pairs.
Standard tuning. Fifth position. Preserve code order; cross after note 3 in Mode A or after note 1 in Mode B.

108 Finger Permutations - Level 4
Three-String Relay: 1+2+1 Two-Crossing Control
Level 3 moved one adjacent-string crossing. Level 4 adds a second crossing while keeping the fret position and string spacing fixed.
1. Same fretting map
1 = index / fret 5
2 = middle / fret 6
3 = ring / fret 7
4 = pinky / fret 8
The four-digit code stays unchanged.
2. New movement rule
Code note 1: first string
Code notes 2-3: middle string
Code note 4: third string
Move through adjacent three-string groups.
There is still no string skip.
3. Picking objective
Crossings occur after notes 1 and 3.
A downstroke start makes both landings upstrokes.
An upstroke start makes both landings downstrokes.
Keep both landings even and relaxed.
Mute every unused string.
Worked example - code 1234
Play note 1 on the first string, notes 2-3 on the middle string, and note 4 on the third string.
ASCEND: E/A/D -> G/B/e

B|--------|--------|------8-|--6-7---|
G|--------|------8-|--6-7---|5-------|
D|------8-|--6-7---|5-------|--------|
A|--6-7---|5-------|--------|--------|
E|5-------|--------|--------|--------|
DESCEND: e/B/G -> D/A/E
e|5-------|--------|--------|--------|
B|--6-7---|5-------|--------|--------|
G|------8-|--6-7---|5-------|--------|
D|--------|------8-|--6-7---|5-------|
A|--------|--------|------8-|--6-7---|
E|--------|--------|--------|------8-|
FIRST PASS
Lightly accent landing notes 2 and 4 so both crossings are deliberate.
SECOND PASS
Remove the accents and make all four notes equal in volume and duration.
Play ASCEND directly into DESCEND without resetting the hands or the pick.

1
Choose one 12-exercise set.
2
Start 10-15 BPM below your clean
Level 3 tempo.
3
Play ASCEND directly into DESCEND.
4
Repeat with the opposite starting
pick stroke.
5
First accent notes 2 and 4; then
equalize all four notes.
6
Three clean loops: add 2 BPM
next session.
7
Two errors or rising tension:
reduce 4-6 BPM.
Advance after the complete set is clean with both pick starts
on two separate days.
Standard tuning. Fifth position. 1+2+1 across three adjacent strings; no string skip or position shift.
Page 1 of 10

108 Finger Permutations - Level 5
One-String-Skip Transfer: 2+2 Gap Crossing and Muting Control
Level 4 connected three adjacent strings. Level 5 restores the familiar 2+2 split so the only new variable is clearing one unused string.
1. Keep the foundation fixed
1 = index / fret 5
2 = middle / fret 6
3 = ring / fret 7
4 = pinky / fret 8
Return to the familiar 2+2 split.
2. Cross one silent string
Ascend: E-D, A-G, D-B, G-e.
Descend: e-G, B-D, G-A, D-E.
Notes 1-2 stay on the source string.
Notes 3-4 land on the target string.
3. Make the gap inaudible
The string between source and target stays silent.
First pass: accent landing note 3.
Second pass: equalize all four notes.
Use both downstroke and upstroke starts.
Worked example - code 1234
Play 1-2 on the source string, clear the middle string, then land 3-4 on the target string.
ASCEND - ONE-STRING SKIPS
DESCEND - ONE-STRING SKIPS

B|--------|--------|----7-8-|--------|
G|--------|----7-8-|--------|5-6-----|
D|----7-8-|--------|5-6-----|--------|
A|--------|5-6-----|--------|--------|
E|5-6-----|--------|--------|--------|
e|5-6-----|--------|--------|--------|
B|--------|5-6-----|--------|--------|
G|----7-8-|--------|5-6-----|--------|
D|--------|----7-8-|--------|5-6-----|
A|--------|--------|----7-8-|--------|
E|--------|--------|--------|----7-8-|
PASS 1
Lightly accent note 3 and listen for accidental contact with the skipped string.
PASS 2
Remove the accent, keep the skipped string silent, and reduce unnecessary pick travel.
Use shallow pick depth; the pick should clear the gap without making a large vertical jump.
Practice protocol
1
Choose one 12-exercise set.
2
Start 10-15 BPM below your clean
Level 4 tempo.
3
Play every exercise up and down
with a downstroke start.
4
Repeat the full set with an
upstroke start.
5
After three clean loops, add
2 BPM next session.
6

Standard tuning. Fifth position. 2+2 split across one silent string; preserve the four-digit code order.
Page 1 of 10

lines.text: 2+2 gap crossing and muting control in standard tuning.
Return to the even 2+2 split so that string skipping is the only new variable.
Play digits 1-2 on the source string and digits 3-4 on the target string, leaving exactly one physical string between them.
Ascend through E-D, A-G, D-B, G-e. Descend through e-G, B-D, G-A, D-E.
The four-digit code order never changes. The skipped middle string must remain silent.
Level 4 trained two crossings across three adjacent strings. Level 5 reduces the code to one crossing but increases the
distance of that crossing. This isolates string-skipping, pick-path, and muting control without adding a position shift.
Begin 10-15 BPM below your clean Level 4 tempo. Use one 12-code set per session.
Play each exercise ascending and descending, once beginning with a downstroke and once beginning with an upstroke.
First pass: lightly accent note 3, the first note after the skip, and listen for accidental skipped-string contact.
Second pass: make all four notes equal in volume, keep the middle string silent, and minimize unnecessary pick travel.
Rotate the existing straight-16th, triplet, and quintuplet groupings across sessions.
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next time. After two noisy skips, errors, or rising tension, reduce 4-6 BPM.
Advance when the complete set is clean with both pick-start directions on two separate days.

108 Finger Permutations - Level 7
Three-String Skip Relay: 1+2+1 Double-Gap Crossing Control
Level 7 combines the three-string relay from Level 4 with the skipped-string landings developed in Levels 5 and 6.
1. Keep the foundation fixed
1 = index / fret 5
2 = middle / fret 6
3 = ring / fret 7
4 = pinky / fret 8
The four-digit code never changes.
2. Relay across every other string
Ascend: E-D-B, then A-G-e.
Descend: e-G-A, then B-D-E.
Note 1 starts; notes 2-3 share the middle.
Note 4 completes the second gap crossing.
3. Make both gaps inaudible
Both intervening strings stay silent.
First pass: accent landing notes 2 and 4.
Second pass: equalize all four notes.
Use both downstroke and upstroke starts.
Worked example - code 1234
Play 1 on the first string, 2-3 on the next played string, and 4 on the third; one silent string separates each landing.
ASCEND - E-D-B / A-G-e
DESCEND - e-G-A / B-D-E
e|--------|------8-|
B|------8-|--------|
G|--------|--6-7---|
D|--6-7---|--------|
A|--------|5-------|
E|5-------|--------|
e|5-------|--------|
B|--------|5-------|
G|--6-7---|--------|
D|--------|--6-7---|
A|------8-|--------|
E|--------|------8-|
PASS 1
Separate the four-note cells; lightly accent notes 2 and 4 and audit both silent strings.
PASS 2
Connect the route, remove the accents, and keep volume, timing, and note length even.
Move diagonally with shallow pick depth; do not turn either gap into a large vertical jump.
Practice protocol
1
Choose one 12-exercise set.
2
Start 10-15 BPM below the slower
of your clean Level 6 modes.
3
Play every exercise up and down
with a downstroke start.
4
Repeat the full set with an
upstroke start.
5
After three clean loops, add
2 BPM next session.
6
After two noisy gaps or tension,
reduce 4-6 BPM; require two clean days.
Standard tuning. Fifth position. 1+2+1 across three played strings; clear one silent string at each crossing.
Page 1 of 10

lines.text: 108 FINGER PERMUTATIONS - LEVEL 7: THREE-STRING SKIP RELAY
1+2+1 double-gap crossing and muting control in standard tuning.
Play code note 1 on the first played string, code notes 2-3 on the middle played string, and code note 4 on the third.
Leave one physical string silent between the first and middle played strings and another silent string between the middle
and third played strings. Ascend through E-D-B and A-G-e. Descend through e-G-A and B-D-E.
The 1+2+1 description refers to note counts, not finger numbers. The four-digit code order never changes.
Level 4 introduced the 1+2+1 relay across adjacent strings. Levels 5 and 6 trained one skipped-string crossing at
different rhythmic points. Level 7 combines those skills: both crossings in the relay now clear a silent string.
This doubles the number of skipped-string landings per code without adding a position shift or a wider individual leap.
Use one 12-exercise set per session. Begin 10-15 BPM below the slower of your two clean Level 6 modes.
Play ASCEND directly into DESCEND, then repeat the entire exercise with the opposite starting pick stroke.
First pass: separate the four-note cells, use short notes, and lightly accent landing notes 2 and 4.
Verify that both intervening strings remain silent and that neither crossing becomes an exaggerated vertical jump.
Second pass: connect the route, remove the accents, and equalize all four notes in volume, timing, and duration.
Use straight 16ths first. Reintroduce triplet and quintuplet groupings only after both gap landings are stable.
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next session. After two noisy gaps, errors, or rising tension, reduce 4-6 BPM.
Advance after the full set is clean with both pick starts on two separate days.

108 Finger Permutations - Level 8
Two-Position Ladder: 4+4 Whole-Pattern Shift Control
Level 8 begins the horizontal-mobility branch. String-crossing difficulty is intentionally removed so the hand can learn one new task: release, relocate, and rebuild the four-fret frame without losing
time.
1. Keep two fret frames fixed
P5: 1=5, 2=6, 3=7, 4=8.
P7: 1=7, 2=8, 3=9, 4=10.
Use the assigned finger in both frames.
Do not stretch from P5 to fake the move.
2. Echo the complete code
Play all four digits in P5.
Shift the hand two frets as one unit.
Repeat the same four digits in P7.
Return by reversing the two frames.
3. Make the shift inaudible
Release pressure before moving.
Keep fingertips close to the strings.
Move the thumb with the hand frame.
No scrape, slide, pause, or extra accent.
Worked example - code 1234
The barline is the shift boundary. The aligned one-string template is repeated on each string in the printed route; the notes are not played as a
chord.
SHIFT UP - E > A > D > G > B > e
P5                         P7
S|5-6-7-8----|7-8-9-10---|
SHIFT DOWN - e > B > G > D > A > E
P7                         P5
S|7-8-9-10---|5-6-7-8----|
PASS 1
Play as even eighth notes. Insert one deliberate subdivision at the barline, release pressure, move the whole frame, and lightly
accent the first note after the shift.
PASS 2

1
Choose one 12-exercise set.

Repeat both routes with an upstroke start.
5
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM at the next session.
6
After two late landings, squeaks, or tension, reduce 4-6
BPM; require two clean days.

lines.text: 4+4 whole-pattern position-shift control in standard tuning.
Play the complete four-digit code in fifth position, release pressure, shift the entire hand frame two frets,
and repeat the same code in seventh position. For the return route, play the code in seventh position first,
then shift down and repeat it in fifth position. The shift occurs only between complete four-note cells.
Play SHIFT UP on E-A-D-G-B-e and SHIFT DOWN on e-B-G-D-A-E, one string at a time.
The repeated aligned tab lines are a compact map; they are not simultaneous chord tones.
Levels 1-7 developed vertical movement while the fretting hand remained in fifth position. Level 8 starts the
horizontal-mobility branch. It deliberately removes in-cell string crossing so release pressure, target-fret
accuracy, thumb movement, and hand-frame reconstruction can be learned as separate skills.
Use one 12-exercise set per session. Begin 10-15 BPM below your clean Level 1 same-string tempo.
First pass: play even eighth notes, pause one subdivision at the center barline, and lightly accent the first
note after the shift. Second pass: remove the pause and accent, then convert the 4+4 phrase to straight 16ths.
Play both routes with a downstroke start, then repeat with an upstroke start. Because each cell contains four
notes, the second cell begins with the same pick direction; this keeps the new difficulty in the fretting hand.
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next session. After two late landings, fret squeaks, errors, or rising tension,
reduce 4-6 BPM. Advance after the full set is clean in both directions on two separate days.

108 Finger Permutations - Level 9
Mid-Pattern Position Transfer: 2+2 In-Code Shift Control
Level 8 shifted between complete four-note cells. Level 9 moves the boundary inside the code, after note 2, while the pick stays on one string.
1. Keep both frames exact
P5: 1=5, 2=6, 3=7, 4=8.
P7: 1=7, 2=8, 3=9, 4=10.
Use the assigned finger in each frame.
Do not stretch from the old position.
2. Split every code 2+2
Notes 1-2: starting position.
Release after note 2.
Notes 3-4: destination position.
The digit order never changes.
3. Shift the frame, not the pitch
Move hand and thumb as one unit.
The next note may rise, repeat, or fall.
Land with no slide, scrape, or delay.
Keep the unused strings silent.
Worked example - code 1234
The center divider is the shift boundary. Repeat the one-string template on each string in the printed route.

Play notes 1-2, stop, release pressure, move the hand frame, then play notes 3-4.
Use the stop only to verify a clean release and exact landing; do not drag a finger along the string.
PASS 2
Remove the stop. Play straight eighths, lightly accent note 3, then remove the accent and convert to 16ths.
Use D-U | D-U and U-D | U-D so note 3 begins with the same pick direction as note 1.

lines.text: 108 FINGER PERMUTATIONS - LEVEL 9: MID-PATTERN POSITION TRANSFER
2+2 in-code shifts on one string at a time in standard tuning.
SHIFT UP: play digits 1-2 of the code in P5, release pressure, shift the whole hand frame two frets,
then play digits 3-4 in P7. Repeat on E-A-D-G-B-e, one string at a time.
SHIFT DOWN: play digits 1-2 in P7, shift the whole hand frame down two frets, then play digits 3-4 in P5.
Repeat on e-B-G-D-A-E, one string at a time. The center divider marks the shift after note 2.
The position direction describes the hand frame, not the melodic interval; the next note may rise, repeat, or fall.
Even when the fret numbers overlap, relocate the frame and use the assigned finger rather than stretching.
Level 8 placed the shift between complete four-note codes. Level 9 moves the shift inside each code while keeping
the picking hand on one string. This isolates release timing, target-finger preparation, thumb movement, and
reconstruction of the four-fret frame without adding string-crossing difficulty.
Use one 12-exercise set per session and begin 8-12 BPM below your clean Level 8 continuous tempo.
Pass 1: play notes 1-2, stop, release, relocate, and play notes 3-4. Do not slide along the string.
Pass 2: remove the stop, play straight eighths, lightly accent note 3, remove the accent, then convert to 16ths.
Play both routes with a downstroke start and then an upstroke start: D-U | D-U and U-D | U-D.
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next session. After two missed landings, slides, or rising tension, reduce 4-6 BPM.
Advance after the full set is clean in both directions on two separate days.

108 Finger Permutations - Level 10
Odd-Count Position Transfer: 3+1 / 1+3 Shift-Point Control
Level 9 shifted after note 2. Level 10 moves the relocation to an odd-count boundary while the pick remains on one string.
1. Keep both frames exact
P5: 1=5, 2=6, 3=7, 4=8.
P7: 1=7, 2=8, 3=9, 4=10.
Move the hand and thumb as one unit.
Use the assigned finger after every shift.
Overlapping fret numbers do not cancel the move.
2. Move the shift point
Mode A, 3+1: shift after note 3.
Mode B, 1+3: shift after note 1.
UP moves P5>P7; DOWN moves P7>P5.
The four-digit code order never changes.
3. Keep the pulse independent
Strict alternate picking continues through the shift.
Practice both downstroke and upstroke starts.
Do not reset the pick at the barline.
Remove slide noise, delay, and landing accents.
Mode A - 3+1 Late Shift - code 1234
Digits 1-3 stay in the source frame; digit 4 lands in the destination frame.

S|5-6-7------|10---------|

F|1-2-3------|4----------|

LANDING NOTE: 4
Lightly accent it only while learning the relocation.
PICKING
D-start D-U-D | U    U-start U-D-U | D
Do not restart or reverse the picking cycle at the shift boundary.
Mode B - 1+3 Early Shift - code 1234
Digit 1 starts in the source frame; digits 2-4 continue in the destination frame.

S|7----------|6-7-8------|
LANDING NOTE: 2
Lightly accent it only while learning the relocation.
PICKING

Do not restart or reverse the picking cycle at the shift boundary.

Choose one 12-exercise set and one mode.

Begin 8-12 BPM below your clean Level 9 continuous tempo.

Pass 1: pause at the barline and lightly accent the landing note.
4

lines.text: 108 FINGER PERMUTATIONS - LEVEL 10: ODD-COUNT POSITION TRANSFER
3+1 / 1+3 shift-point control on one string at a time in standard tuning.
Mode A - 3+1 late shift: play digits 1-3 in the source position, release pressure, move the whole hand and thumb,
then play digit 4 in the destination position. The landing note is note 4.
Mode B - 1+3 early shift: play digit 1 in the source position, shift the whole frame, then play digits 2-4
in the destination position. The landing note is note 2.
SHIFT UP moves P5 to P7 and repeats one string at a time in this order: E>A>D>G>B>e.
SHIFT DOWN moves P7 to P5 and repeats one string at a time in this order: e>B>G>D>A>E.
The four-digit finger code never changes. The position direction describes the hand frame, not the melodic interval.
A landing note may rise, repeat, or fall in pitch. Overlapping fret numbers still require a real frame relocation.
Level 9 used a balanced 2+2 split, so each side of the shift contained two picked notes. Level 10 moves the shift
to an odd-count boundary. The fretting-hand release and landing now occur after either one note or three notes,
while strict alternate picking continues without a reset. String crossing remains removed so the new challenge is isolated.
Mode A: downstroke start = D-U-D | U; upstroke start = U-D-U | D.
Mode B: downstroke start = D | U-D-U; upstroke start = U | D-U-D.
The barline marks the position shift only. It does not restart, reverse, or otherwise alter the alternate-picking cycle.
Use one 12-exercise set and one mode per session. Begin 8-12 BPM below your clean Level 9 continuous tempo.
Pass 1: play even eighth notes, pause one subdivision at the shift barline, and lightly accent the landing note.
Pass 2: remove the pause and accent, then connect the cell as straight eighths and finally straight 16ths.
Play SHIFT UP and SHIFT DOWN with a downstroke start, then repeat both routes with an upstroke start.
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next session. After two late landings, slides, squeaks, errors, or rising tension,
reduce 4-6 BPM. Advance after both modes are clean in both directions on two separate days.
Then restore the existing triplet and quintuplet pulses without moving the code-bound shift point to match the beat.
Digits 1-3 stay in the source frame; digit 4 lands in the destination frame.
Picking: D-start D-U-D | U; U-start U-D-U | D. Landing note: 4.

108 Finger Permutations - Level 11
Three-Position Relay: 1+2+1 Double-Shift Control
Our lesson plans go to 11.
Levels 8-10 covered every useful single-shift boundary. Level 11 closes the position branch with two relocations inside every code.
1. Keep three frames exact
P5: 1=5, 2=6, 3=7, 4=8.
P7: 1=7, 2=8, 3=9, 4=10.
P9: 1=9, 2=10, 3=11, 4=12.
Move the hand and thumb as one unit.
Do not stretch across position frames.
2. Relay every code 1+2+1
Note 1: first position frame.
Notes 2-3: middle position frame.
Note 4: third position frame.
UP: P5>P7>P9. DOWN: P9>P7>P5.
The four-digit finger code never changes.
3. Control both landing notes
Landing notes are 2 and 4.
Alternate picking never resets at a shift.
Remove pause, slide noise, and extra accent.
Pitch may rise, repeat, or fall while the
hand frame still moves in the printed direction.
Worked example - code 1234
Each vertical bar is a whole-frame relocation. Repeat the one-string template sequentially on every string in the printed route.
SHIFT UP - E>A>D>G>B>e   P5>P7>P9
SHIFT DOWN - e>B>G>D>A>E   P9>P7>P5
F|1------|2-3----|4------|
F|1------|2-3----|4------|
S|5------|8-9----|12-----|
S|9------|8-9----|8------|
In the DOWN example, fret 8 appears in both P7 and P5. The printed frame and assigned finger remain authoritative.
LANDINGS
Lightly accent notes 2 and 4 only while learning the two relocations.
PICKING
D-start  D | U-D | U     U-start  U | D-U | D
Do not restart, reverse, or exaggerate the picking cycle at either shift boundary.
AFTER MASTERY
Keep the 1+2+1 grouping and vary only the distance: P5>P8>P11 or P5>P7>P10, then reverse.
These are distance variants, not another 108-exercise level.
Session protocol
1
Choose one 12-exercise set.
2
Begin 10-15 BPM below the slower
of your two clean Level 10 modes.
3
Pass 1: use even eighths, pause at
both bars, and accent notes 2 and 4.
4
Pass 2: remove both pauses, then
remove both landing accents.
5
Run UP and DOWN with both pick starts;
use the +2 / -4-6 BPM rule.
6
Advance after 2 clean days; then restore
triplet and quintuplet pulses.
Standard tuning. P5 = frets 5-8; P7 = frets 7-10; P9 = frets 9-12. Shift after notes 1 and 3.

lines.text: 1+2+1 double-shift control on one string at a time in standard tuning.
Divide every four-digit code 1+2+1 across three position frames.
SHIFT UP: play note 1 in P5, release pressure and move the entire hand and thumb to P7, play notes 2-3,
then release and move to P9 for note 4. Repeat one string at a time in this order: E>A>D>G>B>e.
SHIFT DOWN: play note 1 in P9, move the whole frame to P7 for notes 2-3, then move to P5 for note 4.
Repeat one string at a time in this order: e>B>G>D>A>E.
The first landing note is note 2. The second landing note is note 4.
The four-digit finger code never changes, and both frame relocations are mandatory.
Levels 8-10 exhausted the useful single-shift boundaries: after a complete code, after note 2, after note 3,
and after note 1. Level 11 is the horizontal equivalent of the earlier three-part relay levels. It places two
whole-frame relocations inside one four-note cell while keeping the pick on a single string. This closes the
isolated position-shifting section before string changes and position changes are combined.
The direction labels describe the hand frame, not necessarily the melodic contour. A landing pitch may rise,
repeat, or fall. Overlapping fret numbers do not cancel a move. Release, relocate, and use the finger assigned
by the printed position frame rather than stretching or substituting a different fingering.
Both barlines mark fretting-hand shifts only. Do not restart, reverse, or exaggerate the alternate-picking cycle.
Use one 12-exercise set per session. Begin 10-15 BPM below the slower of your two clean Level 10 modes.
Pass 1: use even eighth notes, pause one subdivision at both shift barlines, and lightly accent notes 2 and 4.
Pass 2: remove both pauses while keeping the accents, then remove the accents and equalize all four notes.
Convert the connected cell to straight sixteenth notes. Play SHIFT UP and SHIFT DOWN with a downstroke start,
then repeat both routes with an upstroke start.
After three clean loops, add 2 BPM next session. After two late landings, slides, squeaks, errors, or rising tension,
reduce 4-6 BPM. Advance after the full set is clean in both directions and both pick starts on two separate days.
Then restore the existing triplet and quintuplet pulses without moving either code-bound shift point to match the beat.
Keep the 1+2+1 grouping and vary only the position distance. Examples: P5>P8>P11 or P5>P7>P10, plus their
descending equivalents. These are distance variants of Level 11, not another full 108-exercise level.

lines.text: MAJOR SCALE THREE-NOTE ROLLING SEQUENCE - ONE-OCTAVE NECK LADDER: A TO A
Turn the straight one-octave major scale into overlapping three-note groups. Complete the full
36-note up/down rolling cell, release pressure, move the entire hand-and-thumb frame exactly one fret,
and repeat through every major key. Begin with A major at low-E fret 5, climb to A major at fret 17,
then reverse and return one fret at a time.
WHY THIS LEVEL RETURNS TO ONE OCTAVE
Level 13 expanded the straight scale across two octaves and six strings. Level 14 deliberately returns
to the compact three-string octave so the new sequencing motion can be learned without simultaneously
managing the upper-octave B-string offset. The same rolling sequence can be extended later.
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A major is the starting rung, not the key of every rung.
A fixed-key A-major exercise in every neck position requires changing the note layout and remains a separate branch.
Intervals: whole - whole - half - whole - whole - whole - half
COMPACT ONE-OCTAVE SHAPE - ROOT FRET R ON LOW E
Low E string: R, R+2               Fingers 2,4
A string:     R-1, R, R+2          Fingers 1,2,4
D string:     R-1, R+1, R+2        Fingers 1,3,4
The four-fret hand frame runs from R-1 through R+2.
Each new triplet starts one scale degree farther along. Between groups, the line rolls back one degree:
1-2-3 then 2-3-4; 4-5-6 then 5-6-7. Do not pause or reset at the group boundary.
The complete up/down cell contains 12 triplets and 36 notes. The octave root is repeated at the turn:
the last note of 6-7-8 is followed by the first note of 8-7-6. Because 36 is even, the next key begins
D-start groups: D-U-D | U-D-U | D-U-D | U-D-U ...
U-start groups: U-D-U | D-U-D | U-D-U | D-U-D ...
Do not restart the pick cycle at a new triplet, string crossing, scale turn, or one-fret relocation.
Use eighth-note triplets: one three-note group per beat. Begin 12-18 BPM below your clean Level 13 tempo.

lines.text: MAJOR SCALE THREE-NOTE ROLLING SEQUENCE - TWO-OCTAVE SIX-STRING NECK LADDER: A TO A
Extend the Level 14 three-note rolling sequence across the complete Level 13 two-octave, six-string
major-scale frame. Complete the full 78-note up/down rolling cell, release pressure, move the entire
hand-and-thumb frame exactly one fret, and repeat through every major key. Begin with A major at

Level 14 introduced the overlap pattern inside one octave. Level 15 keeps the exact three-notes-forward,
one-degree-back logic but expands it from 8 scale positions to 15. The sequence now crosses every string,
passes through the middle-octave root, handles the B-string tuning offset, and reaches the high root before
reversing. The extra range is the new difficulty; the scale shape and sequence rule are unchanged.
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A major is the starting rung, not the key of every rung.
A fixed-key A-major exercise in every neck position requires changing the note layout and remains a separate branch.

Turn the compact one-octave major scale into overlapping four-note groups. Complete the full
40-note up/down rolling cell, release pressure, move the entire hand-and-thumb frame exactly
one fret, and repeat through every major key. Begin with A major at low-E fret 5, climb to
A major at fret 17, then reverse and return one fret at a time.
WHY THIS LEVEL RETURNS TO ONE OCTAVE
Level 15 expanded the three-note sequence across two octaves and all six strings. Level 16
deliberately returns to the compact three-string octave so the new four-note overlap can be
learned without simultaneously managing the upper-octave B-string offset. Level 17 can extend
this exact sequence across the complete two-octave frame.
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A major is the starting rung, not the
key of every rung. A fixed-key A-major exercise in every neck position requires changing the
note layout and remains a separate branch.
Intervals: whole - whole - half - whole - whole - whole - half

Low E string: R, R+2               Fingers 2,4
A string:     R-1, R, R+2          Fingers 1,2,4
D string:     R-1, R+1, R+2        Fingers 1,3,4

Extend the Level 16 four-note rolling sequence across the complete two-octave, six-string
major-scale frame. Complete the 96-note up/down cell, release pressure, move the entire
hand-and-thumb frame exactly one fret, and repeat through every major key. Begin with A major
at low-E fret 5, climb to A major at fret 17, then reverse and return one fret at a time.
Level 16 taught the four-note overlap inside the compact one-octave frame. Level 17 keeps the
same overlap and extends it through positions 1-15 across all six strings. This adds the middle
octave, additional string crossings, the B-string tuning offset, and a longer uninterrupted
pick cycle without changing the underlying four-note sequence rule.
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A major is the starting rung, not the
key of every rung. The route passes through all 12 major keys before reaching A one octave

High e:       R-1, R               Fingers 1,2                 Degrees 14,15
The four-fret hand frame runs from R-1 through R+2.
Each new group begins one scale degree farther along. Three notes overlap from one group to
the next. At the boundary, the line drops a diatonic third and resumes forward motion. Do not
pause, accent, or reset at a group boundary.
The complete up/down cell contains 24 groups and 96 notes. The high root is repeated at the
turn: the last note of 12-13-14-15 is followed by the first note of 15-14-13-12. Because 96
is even, the next key begins with the same pick orientation. Because each group has four notes,
every group also begins with the same stroke.

U-start groups: U-D-U-D | U-D-U-D | U-D-U-D ... through all 24 groups.
Never restart the pick cycle at a group, string crossing, octave root, turnaround, or frame shift.
Use sixteenth notes: one four-note group per beat. Begin 15-20 BPM below your clean Level 16
tempo. Master the ascending and descending A-major halves separately, then link them through
the repeated high-root turn. Use 2-3 neighboring rungs and pause one beat after each 96-note
cell. During the pause, release pressure and move the complete frame one fret. Repeat with both
pick starts. Then remove the pause, connect the ladder, reverse at fret 17, and return to fret 5.

dragged shift noise, a crossing accent, a B-string geometry error, or rising tension. Advance

No accumulating shoulder, thumb, wrist, or forearm tension.

LOST SUBDIVISION

Increase route length before increasing speed when the shift is the weak link.
Increase speed before route length when memory is secure but coordination is slow.

5. Remove the accents and use two or three neighboring keys.

lines.text: NATURAL MINOR THREE-NOTE ROLLING SEQUENCE - ONE-OCTAVE NECK LADDER: A TO A
Turn the straight one-octave natural-minor scale into overlapping three-note groups. Complete the full
36-note up/down rolling cell, release pressure, move the entire hand-and-thumb frame exactly one fret,
and repeat through every natural-minor key. Begin with A natural minor at low-E fret 5, climb to A natural
minor at fret 17, then reverse and return one fret at a time.
WHY THIS LEVEL RETURNS TO ONE OCTAVE
Level 22 expanded the straight natural-minor scale across two octaves and all six strings. Level 23
deliberately returns to the compact three-string octave so the new overlap pattern can be learned without
also managing the upper-octave backreach and B-string offset. Level 24 will extend the sequence later.
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A natural minor is the starting rung, not the key of every rung.
A fixed-key A-natural-minor exercise in every neck position requires changing the note layout and remains a separate branch.
Intervals: whole - half - whole - whole - half - whole - whole
COMPACT ONE-OCTAVE SHAPE - ROOT FRET R ON LOW E
Low E string: R, R+2, R+3          Fingers 1,3,4
A string:     R, R+2, R+3          Fingers 1,3,4
The four-fret hand frame runs from R through R+3.

Carry the Level 23 overlapping three-note sequence across the complete two-octave natural-minor frame
from Level 22. Complete the 78-note up/down rolling cell, release pressure, move the entire hand-and-thumb
frame exactly one fret, and repeat through every natural-minor key. Begin with A natural minor at low-E
fret 5, climb to A natural minor at fret 17, then reverse and return one fret at a time.
Level 23 isolated the rolling motion inside one octave. Level 24 preserves the same three-note overlap but
extends it through positions 1-15 and all six strings. The new work is not a new sequence formula; it is
maintaining that formula through the middle octave, the G-string backreach, the B-string tuning offset,
the single high-e endpoint, the repeated high root, and the one-fret relocation.
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A natural minor is the starting rung, not the key
of every rung. A fixed-key A-natural-minor exercise in every neck position requires changing the note layout
and remains a separate later branch.

lines.text: NATURAL MINOR FOUR-NOTE ROLLING SEQUENCE - ONE-OCTAVE NECK LADDER: A TO A
Turn the compact one-octave natural-minor scale into overlapping four-note groups. Complete the full
40-note up/down rolling cell, release pressure, move the entire hand-and-thumb frame exactly one fret,
and repeat through every natural-minor key. Begin with A natural minor at low-E fret 5, climb to A natural
minor at fret 17, then reverse and return one fret at a time.
WHY THIS LEVEL RETURNS TO ONE OCTAVE
Level 24 expanded the three-note rolling sequence across two octaves and all six strings. Level 25
deliberately returns to the compact three-string octave so the new four-note overlap can be learned without
simultaneously managing the upper-octave backreach and B-string offset. Level 26 will extend this exact
sequence across the complete two-octave frame.
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A natural minor is the starting rung, not the key of every rung.
A fixed-key A-natural-minor exercise in every neck position requires changing the note layout and remains a separate branch.
Intervals: whole - half - whole - whole - half - whole - whole

Ascending notes per string: 3-3-2. Descending notes per string: 2-3-3.
Each new group begins one scale degree farther along. At every group boundary, the line drops a diatonic
third and then continues forward. Three notes overlap from one group to the next. Do not pause, accent,
or reset at a group boundary.

DOWN: DDAA | DAAA | AAAE | AAEE | AEEE

the last note of 5-b6-b7-8 is followed by the first note of 8-b7-b6-5. Because 40 is even, the next

U-start groups: U-D-U-D | U-D-U-D | U-D-U-D ... through all 10 groups.
Never restart the pick cycle at a new group, string crossing, scale turn, or one-fret shift.

metronome setting; for example, if Level 24 is clean at 80 BPM, begin near 60 BPM. Master the A-natural-

lines.text: NATURAL MINOR DIATONIC TRIADS - TWO-OCTAVE SIX-STRING NECK LADDER
Level 28 stacks one more scale tone onto the diatonic-thirds idea from Level 27. Every group now plays
a root, third, and fifth: 1-b3-5, 2-4-b6, b3-5-b7, and onward. The exercise converts natural
minor into a connected chain of broken triads while retaining the same two-octave six-string shape
Level 27 isolated two-note thirds and their major/minor qualities. Level 28 adds the diatonic fifth,
turning every interval pair into a complete triad. The mechanical demand becomes a three-note group
that may span one, two, or three strings; the musical demand is to hear and name i, ii diminished,
III, iv, v, VI, and VII without losing the continuous triplet pulse.
Two octaves: 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 b7 8 9 b10 11 12 b13 b14 15
Intervals: whole - half - whole - whole - half - whole - whole, then repeat
Each new triad begins one scale position farther forward. The line climbs a third and another third,
then rolls back three scale positions to begin the next chord. Do not pause or reset at the rollback.
Ascending:  i minor | ii diminished | III major | iv minor | v minor | VI major | VII major | i minor | ii diminished | III major | iv minor
Descending: iv minor | III major | ii diminished | i minor | VII major | VI major | v minor | iv minor | III major | ii diminished | i minor
Natural minor has a minor v and a major VII because degree b7 is not raised. Harmonic minor will alter
those functions later; do not import the raised seventh into this workbook.
TWO-OCTAVE SIX-STRING SHAPE - ROOT FRET R ON LOW E
Low E string: R, R+2, R+3          Fingers 1,3,4        Positions 1,2,b3
A string:     R, R+2, R+3          Fingers 1,3,4        Positions 4,5,b6
D string:     R, R+2               Fingers 1,3          Positions b7,8
G string:     R-1, R, R+2          Fingers 1,2,4        Positions 9,b10,11
B string:     R, R+1, R+3          Fingers 1,2,4        Positions 12,b13,b14
The complete map spans R-1 through R+3. Release and rebuild for the G-string backreach and again for
the B-string offset; do not hold a static five-fret stretch.
Ascending:  EEA | EAA | EAD | AAD | ADG | ADG | DGG | DGB | GGB | GBB | GBe
Descending: eBG | BBG | BGG | BGD | GGD | GDA | GDA | DAA | DAE | AAE | AEE
Some triads remain on two strings, while others span three strings. Keep the middle note rhythmically
centered and every landing equal in volume through the D-G and G-B transitions.
- repeat the high root at the turnaround as the first note of the descending line
- shift the entire hand-and-thumb frame one fret only after the final 5-b3-1 triad

Pulse-control variations
One note per click: assemble the circuit without rhythmic
pressure.
Native pulse: 8ths -> triplets -> 16ths -> 8ths -> triplets.

Complete separate D-start and U-start days.
Use strict alternate picking through all five modules.
Audit the G-string backreach, B-string offset, and high-e

Record one circuit and listen for hidden pick accents.
Do not use economy picking inside this workbook.
Error diagnosis
LOST SUBDIVISION
Return to one note per click, then relink only the failing module
boundary.
WRONG DEGREE ORDER
Speak the numeric sequence before playing; isolate one ascending
or descending half.
RAISED-SEVENTH LEAK
Stop and name b7 aloud; compare natural-minor v and VII before
resuming.
NOISY SHIFT
Release pressure earlier, move the thumb with the hand, and reduce
BPM by 4-6.
PICK RESET
Mute the strings and air-pick the complete note count through the
boundary.
TENSION BUILDUP
Stop the circuit. Shake out, lower the tempo, and use a shorter key
block.
Recovery and advancement rules
After one error: finish the current module, stop, and repair the exact transition.
After two errors: reduce 4-6 BPM or shorten the route to three keys.
After any pain or persistent tension: stop for the day; do not force the full circuit.
Advance 2 BPM only after three clean circuits at the current route length.
Increase route length before speed when the shift is the weak link.
Increase speed before route length when memory is secure but coordination is slow.
A capstone should expose the weak transition, not hide it inside a forced endurance run.

lines.text: NATURAL MINOR SYNTHESIS CIRCUIT - TWO-OCTAVE SIX-STRING NECK LADDER
Level 29 combines the established two-octave natural-minor movements from Levels 22, 24, 26, 27, and 28 into
one uninterrupted circuit. Complete all five modules in the same key before shifting the entire hand-and-thumb
frame one fret. Re-articulate the low root at every module boundary while preserving the alternate-picking cycle.
A. Linear scale:          30 notes - low root to high root, repeat high root, return to low root
B. Three-note roll:       78 notes - 13 ascending triplets and 13 descending triplets
C. Four-note roll:        96 notes - 12 ascending groups and 12 descending groups
D. Diatonic thirds:       52 notes - 13 ascending pairs and 13 descending pairs
E. Diatonic triads:       66 notes - 11 ascending triads and 11 descending triads
Linear -> Three-note roll -> Four-note roll -> Diatonic thirds -> Diatonic triads -> shift one fret
Two octaves: 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 b7 8 9 b10 11 12 b13 b14 15
Intervals: whole - half - whole - whole - half - whole - whole, then repeat
All five module counts are even. With a downstroke start, every module and every new key begins on a downstroke;
with an upstroke start, each begins on an upstroke. Do not reset at group boundaries, string changes, octave turns,
module boundaries, the G-string backreach, the B-string offset, or one-fret shifts.
Learning mode: one note per metronome click through the complete circuit.
1. Learn each module separately in A natural minor.
2. Link adjacent module pairs: A-B, B-C, C-D, and D-E.
3. Play the complete A-natural-minor circuit with a short pause at every module boundary.
4. Remove the pauses while retaining a light accent on each new module root.
5. Remove the accents and use two or three neighboring keys.
6. Complete longer route sections with both a downstroke and an upstroke start.
Down: G# -> G -> F# -> F -> E -> Eb -> D -> C# -> C -> B -> Bb -> A
Do not replay the high A-natural-minor rung during the down pass unless beginning a new round.

Module B makes a wider leap, then resolves to the skipped upper tone. Practice each module separately, link
both modules, then move the complete hand-and-thumb frame exactly one fret. Begin with A major pentatonic
at low-E fret 5, climb to the octave A at fret 17, then reverse and return one fret at a time.

Stop transposing one shape. Keep the key fixed as A major pentatonic and move through five common
positions from the low-E root frame at frets 4-7 through the octave frame at frets 14-17. Learn each
vertical position, connect adjacent positions around one shared anchor note on every string, then link
all five frames in a forward and reverse zigzag.
Pentatonic box numbers vary among methods. This workbook numbers positions in ascending-neck order,
beginning with the A-root frame around low-E fret 5. Use the fret spans, degree maps, and root locations
as the authoritative identity of each position.

Intervals: whole - whole - minor third - whole - minor third

P4 FIFTH-DEGREE FRAME     frets 11-14  starts degree 5  roots A12, G14
P5 SIXTH-DEGREE FRAME     frets 14-17  starts degree 6  roots E17, G14, e17

turn when linking them, producing an even 120-note circuit.

A Major Pentatonic Horizontal String Lanes: controlled shifts, slides, and destination landings
Standard tuning. Fixed key: A major pentatonic. Frets 4-17. Use clean tone before adding gain.
Page 1 of 13
FIXED KEY: A   |   SIX ONE-STRING LANES   |   FRETS 4-17
Turn the five vertical frames from Level 34 into six horizontal melodies. First move with a silent whole-hand relocation, then add one deliberate slide at each seam, and finally land on named targets
over increasing distances.
1. Map the six lanes
Each string contains six A-major-pentatonic notes spanning the five
connected positions. Name the degree before the fret.
2. Separate shift from slide
Module A forbids audible glissando. Module B adds one timed slide and
counts the slide arrival as a sounding note.
3. Land on the destination
Use increasing-distance targets to remove fret fishing. The repeated
target confirms accuracy before the return jump.

1
Say the lane notes and degrees before playing.

Learn one string at a time with silent shifts.
3

Module A: 72 picked notes. Module B: 144 sounding tones but 96 pick attacks because 48 tones arrive by slide. Module C: 96 picked landing notes. Module D: 72 picked snake notes. Total: 384 sounding tones / 336 pick attacks.

A slide is a rhythmic event, not transportation between notes. Its destination must arrive exactly in time.

Fretted-note vibrato

exaggerate string noise. Add gain only after the pitch center,
muting, and attack counts are secure.

lines.text: A MAJOR PENTATONIC EXPRESSIVE ARTICULATION - LEGATO, SLIDES, BENDS, RELEASES, AND VIBRATO
FIXED KEY A - FIVE POSITIONS - FRETS 4-17
Turn the fixed-key A-major-pentatonic map from Levels 34-35 into controlled expressive motion. The pitch map
does not change. What changes is how each pitch begins, connects, bends, releases, and sustains. Train hammer-ons
and pull-offs in all five positions, combine legato with the four shared-anchor seams, calibrate whole-step bends
against named target frets, add pre-bend releases and pitch-centered vibrato, then finish with five short cadences.
Expression does not excuse inaccurate rhythm or pitch. A hammer-on, pull-off, slide arrival, bend target, release,
or vibrato pulse is a timed musical event. Picked and unpicked notes must remain equal in volume and duration.
All core bends in this level are whole-step bends to a note two frets higher. The minor-third gaps 3->5 and 6->1
would require a one-and-a-half-step bend and are deliberately excluded from the core bend module.
Notes: A B C# E F#
h = hammer-on; p = pull-off; / = ascending slide; \ = descending slide; b(T) = bend to target fret T;
r = release; pb(T) = pre-bend silently to target pitch before the attack; ~ = vibrato.
Module A: 5 position cells x 24 sounding tones = 120 tones; 12 attacks per cell = 60 attacks.
Module B: 4 seams x 6 strings x 5 tones = 120 tones; one attack per phrase = 24 attacks.
Module C: 9 whole-step bend sites x 4 attacks = 36 attacks.
Module D: 6 pre-bend cells x 3 attacks = 18 attacks; 8 A-root vibrato holds = 8 attacks.
Module E: 5 cadence phrases = 19 attacks; articulation creates the remaining pitch motion.
Complete core workout: 165 pick attacks, plus 240 explicitly counted legato/slide tones, 15 bend or pre-bend
cells, 8 root-vibrato holds, and 5 cadence phrases.

WEAK HAMMER: strike closer to the fret with less travel; do not squeeze harder with the thumb.
EMPTY PULL-OFF: keep the destination fretted and use a tiny lateral pluck rather than simply lifting.
LATE SLIDE: shorten the motion; the arrival fret is a counted tone, not transportation.
FLAT BEND: support the bending finger, rotate the wrist, and compare directly with the target fret.
SHARP BEND: stop pushing after the target; hold the pitch before adding vibrato.
WIDE VIBRATO: reduce the motion until every pulse returns to the pitch center.
STRING NOISE: mute above the bend with the fretting index and below it with the picking hand.
PAIN OR TENSION: stop. Do not force the whole-step bend or substitute a one-and-a-half-step bend.
Add 2 BPM after three clean runs at the current module length. After two errors, reduce 4-6 BPM or isolate one
string, seam, bend, or cadence. Intonation outranks speed. Use a clean tone until the pitch and muting are stable.

FIXED KEY A - FIVE POSITIONS - A, D, AND E MAJOR HARMONY
Turn the fixed-key A-major-pentatonic map into harmony-aware phrasing. Keep the same five notes and five positions,
but stop treating every note as equally stable. Hear the active I, IV, or V chord; land on a strong chord tone at
the change; use the remaining pentatonic notes as motion; then resolve before the harmony changes again.

I-IV-V chords: A major = A C# E; D major = D F# A; E major = E G# B.

I - A major: A root, C# third, E fifth.

Module D adds D and G# temporarily as chord-completion tones; they are not new pentatonic degrees.

unresolved downbeat landing, until the ear clearly hears the intended color.

OVERFILLED BAR: leave beat 4 empty; silence is part of the phrase.

FIXED KEY A - FIVE POSITIONS - HARMONY A, D, AND E MAJOR
Combine the five fixed-key positions, horizontal movement, expressive articulation, and I-IV-V chord targets
into phrases that sound intentional rather than like scale recitation. Build a short call, leave measured space,
answer the active harmony, develop one recognizable motif, and preserve the chord change while moving across the neck.
Notes: A B C# E F#
I-IV-V chords: A major = A C# E; D major = D F# A; E major = E G# B.
Strong pentatonic targets: A/C#/E over A; F#/A over D; E/B over E.
Completion tones: D* may appear only over D major; G#* may appear only over E major.
A call states a rhythm and contour, then leaves room. It often ends on degree 2 or 6 rather than a final tonic.
A response may echo the rhythm, reverse the contour, move to a neighboring position, or change the chord target.
Silence is counted. A rest is not lost time; it is part of the phrase. A response should arrive because the harmony
changed, not because the player ran out of scale notes.
P = picked attack; h = hammer-on destination; p = pull-off destination; s = slide destination;
b = bend destination; r = rest; = = held tone. Continue alternate picking only through actual picked attacks.
The count row shows eighth-note slots: 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &.

Module B four seam phrases: 97 sounding tones / 62 pick attacks.

positions, cross at least two seams, and use no more than one articulation in each two-bar phrase.
Use all five positions and horizontal lanes. Preserve strong beat-1 targets, include at least two bars of deliberate
space, use D* and G#* only on their supporting chords, and finish on an A root without a last-second fret search.
1 Echo the call rhythm with a new target. 2 Reverse the contour. 3 Move the answer to the next position.
4 Delay the answer by an eighth note. 5 Shorten the answer and leave beat 4 empty. 6 Expand the answer with one
legato, slide, bend, or vibrato event while preserving the target time.
1. Clap and speak the call/response rhythm before touching the guitar.
2. Complete all five local pairs; exaggerate the silence between sentences.
3. Play the four seam phrases and verify every beat-1 target.
4. Perform the seed plus all six transformation options without changing tempo.
5. Play sparse, medium, and dense versions at one unchanged BPM.
6. Learn the 12-bar model chorus in four-bar blocks, then link the full route.
7. Replace only response bars while preserving the written calls.
8. Record the three-chorus capstone and score it before increasing tempo.
CALL AND RESPONSE SOUND IDENTICAL: change one element only - target, contour, position, density, or articulation.
RESPONSE ARRIVES LATE: sing the target before the barline and shorten the call by one note.
NO SPACE: remove beat 4 from every call and one additional beat from every response.
MOTIF DISAPPEARS: keep the rhythm fixed and change only the ending target.
POSITION SHIFT SOUNDS LIKE A BREAK: isolate the final call note, seam movement, and first response target.
BEND OR SLIDE HIDES THE PULSE: remove the articulation; restore subdivision; add it back after timing is clean.
D* OR G#* LEAKS INTO THE WRONG CHORD: return to the five-note pool and rehearse the 12-bar target schedule aloud.
TENSION OR PANIC: stop the free chorus, return to one four-bar phrase, and reduce 4-6 BPM.
Harmony, phrase identity, timing, and pitch control outrank speed. Add 2 BPM after three clean choruses at the
current constraint. After two missed targets or lost phrase boundaries, shorten to four bars or reduce 4-6 BPM.
Use clean tone until the rests, landings, slides, bends, and muting are reliable.
Play all five local pairs and all four seam phrases; transform one motif in six ways; perform sparse, medium, and
dense versions without moving the targets; play the 12-bar model chorus from memory; record the three-chorus
capstone on two separate days; make every chord change audible without accompaniment; use at least one full beat
of deliberate silence in every two-bar pair; use D* and G#* only on IV and V; and end on an A root by choice.
Section V re-centers the same fretboard logic around minor pentatonic and blues vocabulary, beginning with the
relative-minor relationship before adding the blues note, minor-key bends, dominant-blues phrasing, and applications.

A minor pentatonic five-position map and connection
NEW PITCH SET - SAME TONIC: A
1. Hear the new pitch set
A minor pentatonic is A-C-D-E-G: degrees 1-b3-4-5-b7. This
is the parallel minor of A, not the relative minor from Levels
39-40.
2. Learn five positions
Begin with the standard root frame at fret 5. Keep A as tonic
while the starting degree and fretboard geometry change in
every frame.
3. Connect the seams
Adjacent boxes share one anchor note on every string. Shift after that
anchor sounds, then link all five frames into forward and reverse zigzags.

lines.text: A MINOR PENTATONIC FIVE-POSITION MAP AND CONNECTION - FIXED KEY A
Introduce the genuinely new A minor pentatonic pitch set, keep A as the fixed tonic, and connect five common
positions across the neck. Learn each vertical frame, shift only after the shared anchor at every adjacent-position
seam, then link all five boxes in forward and reverse zigzags.

F# minor pentatonic: F# A B C# E   same notes as A major, re-centered in Levels 39-40
A minor pentatonic:  A C D E G     degrees 1 b3 4 5 b7
A minor pentatonic is the parallel-minor pitch collection. It is not the same fret map with renamed degrees.

Intervals: minor third - whole - whole - minor third - whole

PRACTICE PROGRESSION, ERROR REPAIR, AND MASTERY
1. Say the six lane notes and degrees before playing.
2. Learn one Module A lane at one sounding tone per click.
3. Complete all six silent-shift cells with D-start and U-start.
4. Add Module B destination landings; remove fret fishing before increasing speed.
5. Practice one Module C seam, then convert it into the one-pick Module E chain.
6. Complete all five Module D legato cells with equal picked and unpicked volume.
7. Calibrate one whole-step bend against its printed target; then add the release.
8. Establish C# as the blue-third ceiling, then produce a deliberate shade below it.
9. Hold all eight A roots with centered vibrato.
10. Link the five cadence phrases without extra attacks or loss of tonic.
NOISY SHIFT: release earlier, move thumb with hand, reduce 4-6 BPM.
FRET FISHING: look at and name the destination before leaving the launch note.
WEAK HAMMER: strike closer to the fret with less travel; do not clamp the thumb.
EMPTY PULL-OFF: keep the destination fretted and use a tiny lateral pluck.
LATE SLIDE: shorten the motion; the destination is a counted tone.
FLAT OR SHARP BEND: compare directly with the fretted target and hold before releasing.
BLUE SHADE REACHES C#: reduce the motion; the full half-step is only the upper boundary.
WIDE VIBRATO: narrow the movement until every pulse returns to center.
STRING NOISE: mute above the bend with the index and below it with the picking hand.
PAIN OR TENSION: stop. Do not force a bend or hold a rigid five-fret stretch.
Add 2 BPM after three clean runs at the current module length. After two errors, reduce 4-6 BPM or isolate one
lane, seam, bend site, or cadence. Intonation and timing outrank speed. Use clean tone until muting is stable.

A7-D7-E7 chord-tone targeting, guide-tone shells, and twelve-bar voice leading
FIXED KEY: A  |  8 MODULES  |  704 TONES
Level 45 secured the shuffle grid and the twelve-bar form. Level 46 now makes the harmony audible through note choice. The A blues vocabulary remains available, but every chord
change receives an intentional root, third, fifth, or flat seventh. The thirds and flat sevenths become the guide tones that define each dominant chord.
1. Land before filling
Hear and name the next target before the bar arrives.
The fill is optional; the beat-one landing is not.
2. Track the tritone
The third and flat seventh form the dominant guide-tone
shell. Move those voices smoothly through every chord
change.
3. Keep blues color functional

Resolve them when the active chord requires a clearer
target.

A7 -> E7: C#->D and G->G#     both voices rise one half step

Scale Exercises - Section V, Level 47
A major and A minor pentatonic mixing - controlled color over A7-D7-E7
FIXED KEY: A  |  10 MODULES  |  872 TONES
Levels 41-46 established the A-minor map, blues vocabulary, shuffle form, and dominant chord targets. Level 47 adds A-major-pentatonic color without turning the neck into an
undifferentiated eight-note scale. The governing skill is selection: keep the motif and rhythm stable, change one color at a time, and let the active chord determine the landing note.
1. Anchor first
A and E belong to both pentatonic sets. Use one as the
pivot before introducing B, C#, F# or C, D, G.
2. Control the color pairs
C/C# changes the third; F#/G changes 6 versus b7; B/D
changes 2 versus 4. Hear each contrast.
3. Target the chord
A7 welcomes C# and G; D7 needs F# and C; E7 needs
B, D, and the completion tone G#.

SECTION V CAPSTONE - THREE CONNECTED CHORUSES
TURN THE COMPLETE SECTION INTO MUSICAL CONVERSATION

TWELVE-BAR FORM - FIVE POSITIONS - THREE-CHORUS CAPSTONE
Combine the A-minor-pentatonic map, the flat-five blue note, shuffle rhythm, A7-D7-E7 chord targets,
major/minor color control, articulation, position movement, motif development, and deliberate space into
complete musical conversations. The objective is not to play more notes. The objective is to make the form,
the active chord, the motif, the phrase boundary, and the dynamic direction audible without losing the pulse.
A minor pentatonic: A C D E G          degrees 1 b3 4 5 b7
A blues scale:        A C D Eb E G       adds b5
A major pentatonic:   A B C# E F#       degrees 1 2 3 5 6
Completion tone:      G# may appear as the third of E7. F may appear only as a marked chromatic approach.
A call states a rhythm, contour, register, color, or articulation and leaves a question. A response preserves
at least one recognizable feature while changing the chord target, contour, register, density, or ending.
Silence is counted. A position shift must sound like part of the sentence. The strongest target should arrive
because the harmony changed, not because the phrase ran out of notes.
P = picked attack; h = hammer-on; p = pull-off; s = slide arrival; b = bend; b< = blue-third shade;
r = rest; = = held tone. Color row: C common anchor, m minor-only, b5 blue note, M major-only, * completion.
A - local conversations: 57 sounding tones / 38 pick attacks.
B - seam conversations: 92 sounding tones / 77 pick attacks.
C - motif transformations: 47 sounding tones / 30 pick attacks.
D - density ladder: 60 sounding tones / 59 pick attacks.
E - dynamic shape: 60 sounding tones / 57 pick attacks.
F - minor-only chorus: 66 sounding tones / 62 pick attacks.
G - blues/articulation chorus: 71 sounding tones / 46 pick attacks.
H - mixed-color chorus: 75 sounding tones / 68 pick attacks.
I - turnarounds: 60 sounding tones / 57 pick attacks.
J - written recovery: 26 sounding tones / 23 pick attacks.
Complete written workout: 614 sounding tones / 517 pick attacks, before the free capstone.
MODULE A - FIVE LOCAL CALL-AND-RESPONSE PAIRS
P1 - BLUE-NOTE QUESTION, CHORD-TONE ANSWER - P1
Keep the call unresolved. Let the C-to-C# move identify A7 before the final root.
CALL - Ends on the flat seventh after exposing 4-b5-5.
RESPONSE - Turns b3 into the major third, then resolves to A.
P2 - RHYTHMIC ECHO WITH A NEW LANDING - P2
The answer should sound related by rhythm, not copied by pitch.
CALL - Climbs through b3, 4, b5, 5, and b7.
RESPONSE - Preserves the long-short shape and resolves through C# to A.
P3 - REGISTERED CALL, GUIDE-TONE RESPONSE - P3
Do not let the F# become the cadence. The response belongs to A7 only after C# and A arrive.
CALL - Uses the upper-string blue note and resolves it to E.
RESPONSE - Uses F# as color, then states C# and A clearly.
The response reverses direction while preserving the call length and final-bar placement.
CALL - Rises through the chromatic 4-b5-5 cell.
RESPONSE - Falls back through E, C, C#, and A.
P5 - HIGH CALL, TONIC RESET - P5
Hear the minor third as the question and the major third as the answer, not as one continuous chromatic scale.
CALL - Descends from A and leaves the phrase on C.
RESPONSE - Turns C into C#, then resolves high to A.
MODULE B - FOUR CROSS-POSITION SEAM CONVERSATIONS
Route: P1 -> P2 -> P2 -> P1. A lower-frame call is answered in P2, then the V chord points back to the P1 tonic.
Beat-one targets: A | F# | E/G# | C#/A.
Route: P2 -> P3 -> P3 -> P2. Use the fret-9/10 overlap as a route, not as a pause.
Beat-one targets: A | D/F# | E/G# | C#/A.
Route: P3 -> P4 -> P4 -> P3. Let the D7 response establish the upper frame before the E7 call.
Beat-one targets: A | D/F# | E/G# | C#/A.
Route: P4 -> P5 -> P5 -> P4. Reach the highest frame without making the position change sound like a section break.
Beat-one targets: A | D/F# | E/G# | C#/A.
SEED MOTIF: A-C, space, then the 4-b5-5 cell and b7.
1. EXACT ECHO: Repeat the same rhythm, contour, articulation, and ending.
2. RHYTHMIC DISPLACEMENT: Delay the seed by one eighth note without changing the pitch order.
3. CONTOUR REVERSAL: Reverse the direction while preserving the seed pitch family.
4. REGISTER SHIFT: Move the seed into the upper P4/P5 register.
5. MAJOR/MINOR RECOLOR: Keep the rhythm but replace selected minor colors with B, C#, and F#.
6. EXPANSION: Fill the phrase while keeping the seed opening recognizable.
7. REDUCTION: Keep only the tonic, major-third answer, and final tonic.
MODULE D - SPACE AND DENSITY LADDER
SPARSE - THREE TONES PER BAR: One target, one color, one resolution. Count every empty subdivision.
MEDIUM - FIVE TONES PER BAR: Preserve the same beat-one targets while adding a related answer.
DENSE - SEVEN TONES PER BAR: Fill the space without changing the target schedule or accelerating the pulse.
1. QUIET CALL / STRONG ANSWER: The answer is louder because the phrase develops, not because the tempo changes.
Bar 1 p; bar 2 f. Keep the subdivision identical.
2. RISING THREE-PHRASE ARC: Raise register and intensity in three two-bar sentences.
Phrase 1 p, Phrase 2 mf, Phrase 3 f. Do not rush the high-register climax.
3. HIGH CLIMAX / LOW RESOLUTION: Begin high and strong, then descend in register and dynamic level.
Use a real diminuendo: f -> mf -> mp -> p.
MODULE F - MODEL CHORUS 1: MINOR PENTATONIC ONLY
Use only A, C, D, E, and G. The form and phrase structure must remain audible without the blue note or major color.

MODULE G - MODEL CHORUS 2: BLUES SCALE AND ARTICULATION

MODULE H - MODEL CHORUS 3: MAJOR/MINOR MIXTURE AND CHORD TARGETING
Mix color deliberately. C# belongs strongly to A7, F# to D7, and G# only to E7.
BAR 1 - A7 CALL - P1 - beat-1 target A root
BAR 2 - A7 RESPONSE - P2 - beat-1 target C# third
BAR 3 - A7 CALL - P2 - beat-1 target G flat seventh

MODULE I - TURNAROUND AND RE-ENTRY DRILLS
1. LOW TONIC CLOSE: Close the performance instead of launching another chorus.
2. LOW E7 RE-ENTRY: Use G# and B only after the E7 bar begins.
Final destination: E; next chorus begins on A.
3. MID-NECK GUIDE-TONE TURN: Connect C# over A7 to D/G# over E7.
Hear 3 of A7 become b7/3 of E7.
4. HIGH BLUES TURN: A high blue-note gesture resolves to the V chord.
Do not sustain Eb across the E7 downbeat.
5. STOP-TIME RE-ENTRY: Leave beat 4 empty, then enter on the final eighth-note pickup.
The silence must keep counting; the pickup is not guessed.
6. CHROMATIC V APPROACH: Use the support note F as a one-time lower approach to E.
F is marked as a chromatic support tone, not a new blues-scale degree.
MODULE J - ERROR RECOVERY AND MOTIF SALVAGE
A7: C (b3) -> C# (3). Raise or slide one fret.
A7: D (11) -> C# (3). Move down one fret.
A7: F# (13) -> E (5). Move to the nearest fifth.
A7: B (9) -> C# (3). Continue upward one whole step.
D7: C# (M7) -> C (b7). Move down one fret.
D7: G (11) -> F# (3). Move down one fret.
D7: B (13) -> A (5). Move down a whole step.
D7: E (9) -> F# (3). Move up a whole step.
E7: G (#9) -> G# (3). Move up one fret.
E7: A (11) -> G# (3). Move down one fret.
E7: C (b13) -> B (5). Move down one fret.
E7: C# (13) -> B (5). Move down a whole step.
A7 - b3 TO 3: Do not stop after the C; resolve immediately to C# and continue.
D7 - 11 TO 3: Treat G as a passing color and land F#.
E7 - #9 TO 3: Resolve G to G# without changing the rhythm.
LATE RESPONSE - REDUCE: If the full answer is late, play one target and leave the rest open.
MISSED BEND - SOURCE RELEASE: Return to C, then resolve through C# rather than forcing the bend.
LOST POSITION - TONIC RESET: Find any A, leave space, then resume in the nearest secure frame.
MODULE K - THREE-CHORUS CONTROLLED IMPROVISATION CAPSTONE
Use A minor pentatonic only. Maximum four sounding tones per bar. Use no more than two positions. Leave at
least one full beat of silence in every two-bar pair. Make bars 5 and 9 audible through D or E targets.
CHORUS 2 - BLUES VOCABULARY AND MOTIF DEVELOPMENT
Add Eb, slides, legato, bends, releases, and vibrato. Choose one seed motif and transform it in every two-bar
pair. Move through at least four positions. Use no more than one conspicuous articulation per bar.
Mix major and minor pentatonic color. Target C# over A7, F# or C over D7, and G#/B/D/E over E7. Use all
five positions, include a dynamic climax, and choose either a tonic close or a functional E7 turnaround.
Echo: preserve rhythm. Reverse: invert contour. Reposition: answer in the next box. Delay: enter one eighth later.
Reduce: use fewer notes. Expand: add one articulation. Recolor: major versus minor. Target: change only the landing.
Bar 1 A7: beginning. Bar 5 D7: first change. Bar 7 A7: return. Bar 9 E7: top of the form. Bar 11 A7:
tonic return. Bar 12 E7 or A7: turnaround or close. If lost, stop playing, keep counting, and re-enter at the
next landmark instead of inventing an extra measure.
Bend and slide intonation: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Recovery after an error: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Maximum 16. Section-completion standard: 13 or higher on two separate days, with no zero in form awareness,
1. Clap the call-and-response rhythms and count every rest.
2. Complete all five local pairs; exaggerate the phrase boundary.
3. Play all four seam conversations and verify every beat-one target.
4. Transform the seed motif in seven ways without changing tempo.
5. Perform sparse, medium, and dense passes at one BPM.
6. Perform the three dynamic-shape exercises without changing subdivision.
7. Learn each model chorus in four-bar blocks, then play all twelve bars.
8. Replace one response bar at a time while preserving the written calls.
9. Practice tonic closes and E7 re-entries until bar 12 has a clear purpose.
10. Record the three-chorus capstone, score it, repair one category, and record again.
Perform all five local pairs and four seam conversations; transform one motif in seven ways; preserve targets
through sparse, medium, and dense passes; play all three model choruses; execute both a tonic ending and a
functional turnaround; recover from a deliberate wrong note without stopping; record three connected choruses
on two separate days; make the A7-D7-E7 form audible without accompaniment; and score at least 13/16.
Section VI begins harmonic minor. Natural minor degree b7 is raised to 7, creating the minor-key dominant,
the augmented-second interval between b6 and 7, and a new set of chord-tone and phrasing demands.

Level 49 established clean open-chord formation. Level 50 keeps the same shapes but compresses the time available for each change. The new priority is transition economy: planted

4. HOVER     moving fingers stay close to the strings
5. LAND      bass-side or guide destination arrives first
6. VERIFY    correct bass string, chord quality, and muted strings

Guitar Exercises - Section VI, Level 51
Barre pressure, index placement, and release mechanics
MINIMUM PRESSURE  |  NO DEATH GRIP
MOVE THE INDEX AND ARM BEFORE ADDING MORE THUMB PRESSURE
1. Place near the fret
The index lies just behind the fret wire. Roll slightly toward its
thumb-side edge. Avoid placing the soft center of every joint
directly over a string.
2. Add arm support
Let the fretting arm draw the neck lightly toward the body
while the picking arm stabilizes the guitar. The thumb guides;
it does not crush.
3. Solve one dead string
Pick the failed string alone. Shift index angle or vertical
position by a few millimeters. Do not respond by squeezing
every finger harder.

Count|1----2----3----4----|1----2----3----4----|

Sound|ring mute ring mute |ring mute ring mute |

Stop conditions
Normal effort can feel unfamiliar, but sharp pain, tingling, numbness, burning, or lingering hand tension is a stop signal. Shake out the hand, shorten the chord, move higher on the neck, or end the
session.

Guitar Exercises - Section VI, Level 53
Major and minor triads across all four adjacent three-string sets
4 STRING SETS  |  1248 ATTACKS + 168 SILENT FORMATIONS
Level 52 established root position, first inversion, and second inversion on G-B-e. Level 53 keeps the same triad spelling and inversion logic while moving the harmony through D-G-B,
A-D-G, and E-A-D. The new challenge is not learning different chord qualities; it is preserving voice identity, muting, and nearest movement as the string register changes.
1. Keep the inversion name
The lowest string of the active set is the bass. Name
whether it carries root, third, or fifth before attacking.
2. Move the three-string window
Mute every string outside the selected set. The chord
must sound like three named voices, not a partial barre
with leakage.
3. Choose register deliberately
The same chord and inversion can appear in several
octaves. Select the string set that supports the rhythm
part, melody, or lead fragment.
Four adjacent string sets
SET 1-2-3   G-B-e   already introduced in Level 52
SET 2-3-4   D-G-B   crosses the G-to-B tuning offset
SET 3-4-5   A-D-G   three perfect-fourth string gaps
SET 4-5-6   E-A-D   same geometry as A-D-G
TRIAD ORDERS
Major: root 1-3-5 | first 3-5-1 | second 5-1-3
Minor: root 1-b3-5 | first b3-5-1 | second 5-1-b3

lines.text: CAGED AS A PRACTICAL CHORD, TRIAD, ROOT, ARPEGGIO, AND NEARBY-SCALE MAP

Use CAGED as an indexing system rather than a five-grip memorization doctrine. Each form identifies root locations, a useful chord fragment, embedded triads, a chord-tone arpeggio, and nearby scale tones. Full C and G forms are optional; partial voicings and triads are the primary performance material.
COMPLETE SOUNDED WORKOUT: 558 attacks plus 45 silent formation prompts.
C form open -> A form fret 3 -> G form fret 5 -> E form fret 8 -> D form fret 10 -> next C form fret 12.
C form: A-string root r; x r r-1 r-3 r-2 r-3. Additional root on B string r-2.
A form: A-string root r; x r r+2 r+2 r+2 r. Additional root on G string r+2.
G form: low-E root r; r r-1 r-3 r-3 r-3 r. Additional roots on G string r-3 and high e r.
E form: low-E root r; r r+2 r+2 r+1 r r. Additional roots on D string r+2 and high e r.
D form: D-string root r; x x r r+2 r+3 r+2. Additional root on B string r+3.
MODULE A - ROOT MAP AND SILENT FORMATION

For each natural root C-D-E-F-G-A-B, form the C, A, G, E, and D regions silently. Use an octave that keeps all required frets on the fingerboard. Name every root in the form, release, then verify one practical partial and one triad.
Silent count: 5 master forms + 5 practical partials + 35 root/form prompts = 45.
MODULE B - FIVE C-MAJOR FORM FAMILIES
C FORM - C FORM - OPEN/ROOT-SIDE MAP - open-3
The open form is practical as a full chord. Keep the unused low E muted and treat the A-D-G-B fragment as the main movable reference.
A-D-G root position: strings A-D-G frets 3-2-0 degrees 1-3-5 inversion RP.
D-G-B first inversion: strings D-G-B frets 2-0-1 degrees 3-5-1 inversion 1st.
G-B-e second inversion: strings G-B-e frets 0-1-0 degrees 5-1-3 inversion 2nd.
A FORM - A FORM - LOW-MIDDLE BARRE MAP - 3-7
The full A-form barre is useful, but the A-D-G-B fragment usually gives cleaner pressure and better access to nearby triads.
G-B-e root position: strings G-B-e frets 5-5-3 degrees 1-3-5 inversion RP.
D-G-B second inversion: strings D-G-B frets 5-5-5 degrees 5-1-3 inversion 2nd.
A-D-G first inversion: strings A-D-G frets 7-5-5 degrees 3-5-1 inversion 1st.
G FORM - G FORM - LOW-REGISTER FRAGMENT MAP - 5-8
The full G form is an orientation shape, not a required grip. Use E-A-D-G and the embedded triads as the practical musical material.
E-A-D root position: strings E-A-D frets 8-7-5 degrees 1-3-5 inversion RP.
A-D-G first inversion: strings A-D-G frets 7-5-5 degrees 3-5-1 inversion 1st.
D-G-B second inversion: strings D-G-B frets 5-5-5 degrees 5-1-3 inversion 2nd.

Guitar Exercises - Section VI, Level 55
Diatonic major-key harmony, Roman numerals, progression families, and transposition
6 KEYS  |  11 MODULES  |  936 ATTACKS
The chord shapes from Levels 49-54 now become a harmonic language. Build a triad on every major-scale degree, label its quality with Roman numerals, group the chords by function,
and move the same progression through several keys without changing its numerical identity.
1. Harmonize the scale

and vii°.
2. Hear function
Tonic chords stabilize; predominant chords prepare;
dominant chords create return pressure.
3. Transpose by number

names, roots, and key signatures change.

Guitar Exercises - Section VI, Level 57
Major 7, dominant 7, minor 7, half-diminished, shells, ii-V-I, and functional voice leading
4 QUALITIES  |  56 SILENT FORMS  |  796 ATTACKS
Level 56 established natural-minor and raised-seventh dominant function. Level 57 adds the seventh to each triad, introduces practical movable four-note voicings, reduces them to shell
voicings, and connects thirds and sevenths through major ii-V-I, minor iiø-V-i, and A-blues progressions.
1. Hear the seventh
The seventh changes function and color: major 7, flat 7,
or half-diminished tension.
2. Reduce to the shell
Root, third, and seventh identify most seventh-chord
function. Add the fifth only when quality requires it.
3. Move voices, not blocks
Track thirds and sevenths by half step or common tone
before adding roots, fifths, or rhythm patterns.
Four seventh-chord qualities
MAJOR 7          1-3-5-7       bright tonic / color chord
DOMINANT 7       1-3-5-b7      active dominant; tritone between 3 and b7
MINOR 7          1-b3-5-b7     minor tonic, predominant, modal color
MINOR 7 b5       1-b3-b5-b7    half-diminished predominant in minor
MAJOR ii-V-I     m7  -> 7  -> maj7
MINOR iiø-V-i    m7b5 -> 7 -> m7
SHELL LIMITATION: m7 and m7b5 share the same R-b3-b7 shell.
The flat fifth must be added or heard elsewhere to identify half-diminished quality.

Guitar Exercises - Section VI, Level 58
Sixteenth-note rhythm guitar, syncopation, dead strokes, releases, and full-song comping
9 MODULES  |  1018 CONTACTS
Levels 49-57 built the chord vocabulary. Level 58 turns it into continuous sixteenth-note rhythm guitar. The right hand maintains the 1-e-&-a motion while the left hand decides whether
each stroke produces a pitched chord, a dead sound, a tie, a pressure release, or no string contact.
1. Keep the motor running
Downstrokes occur on numbers and ampersands;
upstrokes occur on e and a. Air strokes remain part of
the motion.
2. Separate contact from sound
A dead stroke is a deliberate string contact. A tie or air
stroke creates no new attack. Do not confuse the three.
3. Phrase the full song
Different sections use different density, register, muting,
and dynamics while the pulse and form remain
continuous.
Sixteenth-note movement and sound symbols
Cnt|1e&a|2e&a|3e&a|4e&a|
Hnd|DUDU|DUDU|DUDU|DUDU|
P = pitched chord attack
x = dead / muted strum
- = air stroke; no string contact
~ = tie or sustain; no new attack
R = left-hand pressure release
> = accent the following contact

Module
Contacts

TOTAL

Session protocol
Clap and air-strum every new pattern before adding a chord. Use partial voicings when full chords create unwanted strings. Record the right hand from the picking-side angle and verify that the
motion continues through rests and ties.
SAFETY
Keep the wrist loose, the pick shallow, and the forearm free of rigid sixteenth-note pumping. Stop if tension builds.
Standard tuning. Sixteenth-note rhythm guitar, syncopation, dead strokes, releases, anticipations, and full-song comping.

Attack-zone rule
Full open chords may use five or six strings. Funk and dead-stroke patterns usually work better
with three- or four-string partials. Choose the smallest voicing that communicates the harmony.
Accent rule
Create an accent with velocity and timing, not by burying the pick deeper between the strings.
The unaccented contacts must remain controlled and audible.
