Guitar Exercises - Section VII, Level 59
Major and minor triad arpeggios, inversion starts, and picking systems
SECTION VII START  |  1120 ATTACKS
Section VI built chords and triads as simultaneous voicings. Level 59 turns those same three notes into ordered melodic structures. Every arpeggio must preserve chord spelling,
separation, muting, picking continuity, and the active harmonic target.
1. Hear the chord inside the line
Block the triad first, then separate the same notes. The
arpeggio is a chord unfolded in time.
2. Start from every inversion
Root, third, or fifth may be the lowest note. Inversion
identity must remain audible during the route.
3. Compare picking systems
Strict alternate picking crosses every string
independently. Economy picking follows the string
direction without becoming a strum.

SECTION VII  |  4 QUALITIES  |  1,440 ATTACKS
Level 59 separated triads into melodic lines. Level 60 adds the seventh, expands the arpeggio to four strings, and develops strict alternate picking, directional economy picking,
controlled sweep motion, guide-tone emphasis, major ii-V-I tracking, minor iiø-V-i tracking, and chord-to-scale connections.

complete spelling before the first attack.
2. Separate a sweep from a strum
Each string must stop before the next begins. The pick
moves continuously; the fretting hand prevents overlap.
3. Hear the guide tones
The third and seventh carry function. Accent them before
adding roots, fifths, scales, or speed.

Guitar Exercises - Section VII, Level 61
Chord-tone soloing, chromatic approaches, enclosures, delayed resolution, and progression-specific phrases
10 MODULES  |  816 TONES
Level 60 established seventh-chord arpeggios. Level 61 turns those shapes into melodic phrases. Chord tones define the destination; diatonic and chromatic notes create motion;
enclosures frame a target; delayed resolutions create tension without losing the progression.
1. Name the destination
Choose the chord and target before selecting the
approach. A phrase without a destination is only a note
collection.
2. Approach, do not replace
Chromatic and diatonic neighbors lead into a chord tone.
They do not become equal resting points.
3. Resolve on purpose
Land early, late, or through an enclosure because the
phrase demands it, not because the hand found a
nearby fret.
Core phrase grammar
TARGET FIRST       target - fill - space
APPROACH BELOW     below* -> target
APPROACH ABOVE     above* -> target
ENCLOSURE          above* -> below* -> target
DELAYED RESOLUTION tension on beat 1 -> target on & or beat 2
MAJOR ii-V-I       ii m7 -> V7 -> I maj7
MINOR iiø-V-i      ii m7b5 -> V7 -> i m7
* approach notes are temporary unless they also belong to the active chord or key.

10 MODULES  |  788 TONES  |  FRETS 0-20
Level 61 taught approaches, enclosures, delayed resolutions, and progression-specific phrase construction. Level 62 stretches those harmonic ideas across the full neck. The player
must preserve chord identity while skipping strings, changing position, beginning from different inversions, and developing a motif over longer distances.
1. See the landing first
Name the destination note, role, string, and fret before

Register and contour may change, but the chord role and
motif schedule must remain recognizable.
Core phrase architecture
DIAGONAL FRAGMENT   chord tone -> higher string -> new fret region
STRING SKIP         current note -> silent string -> destination note
POSITION SHIFT      release -> relocate -> land; no glissando unless marked
INVERSION START     3, 5, 7, b3, b5, or b7 may begin the arpeggio
MAJOR FUNCTION      Dm7 -> G7 -> Cmaj7
MINOR FUNCTION      Bm7b5 -> E7 -> Am7
MOTIF RULE          preserve rhythm, role schedule, or contour across the shift

1. Hear and name the target.

3. Release excess pressure.
4. Move thumb and hand together.

String-skip mechanics
The pick leaves the current string and travels directly to the destination string. The skipped
string remains silent. Reduce pick depth, pre-locate the destination, and mute unused strings
with both hands.
FAILURE
sweep noise, delayed landing, or a visible search for the next string

Adjacent strings: alternate or controlled economy.
Skipped strings: independent pick attacks.
Odd-note loops: starting stroke reverses next repetition.
Long shifts: preserve the stroke cycle through the move.
Muted preview: air-pick the route before sounding it.

Level 62 connected arpeggio fragments diagonally across the neck. Level 63 broadens the right-hand vocabulary while preserving the same harmonic clarity. Crosspicking keeps
alternate strokes moving through multi-string rolls; hybrid picking separates pick and fingers; sweep bursts compress adjacent-string motion; endurance work tests whether tone, muting,
and time survive repetition.
1. Cross the strings cleanly
Use a curved alternate-picking path. Every string change
receives one independent attack and the previous string
stops ringing.
2. Assign pick and fingers
The pick controls the lower voice; middle and ring
fingers articulate upper voices without changing the
phrase rhythm.
3. Sweep only in bursts
One motion crosses adjacent strings, but every note
remains separate. Release each fret before the next
string sounds.

Session protocol
Choose one crosspicking cell, one hybrid cell, and one sweep burst. Stop before fatigue changes the attack. Rest at least as long as the work interval during endurance training. A faster phrase is
not successful if notes overlap, skipped strings ring, or the chord identity disappears.

Muting responsibilities
Fretting hand releases the completed string. Picking-hand palm or spare fingers silence lower
strings. The active note should be the only sustained pitch unless a printed pedal tone is
intentional.
Volume responsibilities
Reduce pick volume until m and a can match it comfortably. Do not solve a weak finger-plucked
note by snapping the string or tensing the hand.
Sweep-release sequence
FRET -> ATTACK -> RELEASE -> NEXT STRING
         one pitch at a time
         no held mini-barre unless printed
Endurance boundary
Work intervals begin at 15 seconds. Rest for the same duration. Increase time only after tone
and muting remain unchanged through the final repetition.
STOP CONDITION
Pain, burning tension, uncontrolled string noise, or a collapsing pick grip ends the set immediately.

Dynamic and density arc
Bars 1-4: p and sparse. Bars 5-8: mp with one repeated roll. Bars 9-12: mf with wider register.

Recovery cards
Crosspick catches string -> simplify to three-note roll
Hybrid finger misses -> continue with pick-only target
Sweep overlaps -> stop burst on highest clean note
Pick cycle lost -> use next target as new downstroke
Fatigue appears -> insert full-beat rest and reduce density
Phrase-construction limits
Use no more than two picking systems inside one four-bar phrase. Keep one recognizable
arpeggio contour. Land on a chord tone at every harmonic change. Leave at least one full-beat
rest per four bars.
Final recorded assignment
Record one major and one minor sixteen-bar performance. The first take follows the printed systems. The second chooses systems by musical function. Evaluate tone equality, note separation, muting,
tempo, chord identity, dynamic shape, and recovery.
PASS
The second performance must sound more musical, not merely more technically varied.

Guitar Exercises - Section VIII, Level 65
A harmonic minor construction, leading-tone control, dominant harmony, and diminished resolution
FIXED KEY: A  |  10 MODULES  |  652 TONES
Section VIII begins by changing one note of A natural minor: G becomes G#. That raised seventh creates the leading tone, the strong E or E7 dominant, the G# diminished leading-tone
chord, and the characteristic augmented second between F and G#. The objective is controlled function, not exotic-sounding scale runs.
1. Hear the leading tone
G# is not merely a raised fret. It must pull toward A and
identify E or E7 when the dominant is active.
2. Control the augmented second
F to G# spans three semitones. Practice it slowly so the
interval sounds intentional instead of like a missed scale
step.
3. Connect scale and harmony
Am, Dm, E7, G#dim, and G#dim7 provide the structural
destinations for the new scale color.

Guitar Exercises - Section VIII, Level 68
E Phrygian dominant, diminished-seventh symmetry, dominant tension colors, and improvisation synthesis
A HARMONIC MINOR  |  11 MODULES  |  630 TONES
Level 67 mapped the harmonic-minor modes and their chord functions. Level 68 turns the dominant region into a complete improvisation system: E Phrygian dominant, E7b9, the G#dim7
upper structure, diminished symmetry, borrowed #9 color, cadence construction, call and response, and long-form resolution.
1. Hear E7 inside the mode
E Phrygian dominant is E-F-G#-A-B-C-D. The chord tones
E-G#-B-D must remain audible beneath the b9, 11, and
b13 colors.
2. Use diminished symmetry functionally
G#dim7 repeats every three frets. The shape may rotate,
but in A minor its job remains leading-tone resolution or
the upper structure of E7b9.
3. Budget the tension
Add b9, borrowed #9, 11, or b13 one at a time. Combine
them only after the destination chord and final target
remain clear.

Guitar Exercises - Section IX, Level 69
A melodic minor construction, raised sixth and seventh control, tonic colors, and new chord harmony
FIXED KEY: A  |  10 MODULES  |  640 TONES
Section IX begins by changing the upper half of A natural minor. Harmonic minor raised only the seventh; melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh. The result removes the
augmented second, strengthens the leading tone, creates a major IV chord, and introduces a new seventh-chord family.
1. Hear the three minor forms
Natural, harmonic, and melodic minor differ only in
degrees 6 and 7. Compare them before learning new
fretboard geometry.
2. Control F/F# and G/G#
The raised sixth and raised seventh must be deliberate.
Do not let the direction of the line choose them
automatically.
3. Hear the new harmony
Melodic minor creates Bm7, D7, F#m7b5, and G#m7b5
while retaining AmMaj7, Cmaj7#5, and E7.

Two directional conventions
Symmetric or modern/jazz melodic minor uses A-B-C-D-E-F#-G# in both directions. Classical melodic minor commonly ascends with F# and G# but descends as natural minor with G and F. This
workbook trains both choices and labels them explicitly.

lines.text: A MELODIC MINOR SCALE CONSTRUCTION, RAISED SIXTH AND SEVENTH CONTROL, TONIC COLORS, AND SEVENTH-CHORD HARMONY

Introduce A melodic minor by comparing it directly with natural and harmonic minor. Control F/F# and G/G#, train symmetric and classical descending options, develop AmMaj7/Am6 tonic colors, harmonize the scale in triads and seventh chords, and apply the new harmony through progression phrases and a long-form capstone.
A natural minor:  A B C D E F  G  A   = 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 b7 1
A harmonic minor: A B C D E F  G# A   = 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 7  1
A melodic minor:  A B C D E F# G# A   = 1 2 b3 4 5 6  7  1
Symmetric / modern: use A melodic minor ascending and descending.
Classical: ascend with F# and G#; descend through A natural minor with G and F.

Stacking diatonic thirds on scale degree 7 produces G#-B-D-F#: G#m7b5. In the parent A-minor
system, it can resolve by half-step motion into AmMaj7.
Applied altered-dominant reading
When G# is treated as a dominant root, C is respelled B# as the major third. The same pitch
collection becomes G# altered and points toward C# major or minor.
PRACTICE ORDER
Chord arpeggio -> one-octave mode -> characteristic note -> destination chord.
WARNING
Do not apply altered-scale tension to G#m7b5 unless the harmony has actually been reinterpreted as G#7alt.

altered. Their shared tritone explains direct dominant and tritone-substitute resolution into C# minor.
1. Hear D7#11
D Lydian dominant combines a complete D7 shell with
the raised fourth G# and the color tones E and B.
2. Control G#7alt
G# altered contains every altered ninth and fifth around
the dominant shell. The target chord explains the
spelling.
3. Compare two dominants
G#7alt and D7#11 share C-F#. One is the direct
dominant; the other approaches C# minor by tritone
substitution.

A melodic minor: A B C D E F# G#
G# A B C D E F# | 1 b9 #9 3 b5 #5 b7 | G#7alt
D7#11 roles: D root, E 9, F# 3, G# #11, A 5, B 13, C b7.
G#7alt roles: G# root, A b9, B #9, C/B# 3, D b5, E #5, F# b7.
Direct voice leading: B#->C#, F#->E, A->G#, E common.
Substitute voice leading: D->C#, F#->E, C->B, G# common.
MODULE A - D LYDIAN DOMINANT MIRRORS
MODULE B - D7#11 COLOR AND RESOLUTION CELLS
MODULE D - G#7ALT RESOLUTION INTO C# MINOR
D1 - b9 and major 3 to tonic
D5 - b7 falling to tonic b3
D6 - major 3 rising to tonic root
MODULE F - DIRECT DOMINANT VERSUS TRITONE-SUBSTITUTE CADENCES
MODULE G - APPLIED DOMINANT PHRASES IN C# MINOR
MODULE H - PARENT, APPLIED, SUBSTITUTE, AND MINOR-CADENCE COMPARISONS
H1 - parent dominant to A minor
MODULE I - TRANSPOSED TRITONE-SUBSTITUTION GUIDE-TONE CELLS
MODULE J - SIXTEEN-BAR MELODIC-MINOR DOMINANT-SYNTHESIS SOLO
MODULE K - RECOVERY CARDS AND THREE-PASS CAPSTONE
G#7alt: D -> C# | b5 -> tonic R
G#7alt: F# -> E | b7 -> tonic b3
CAPSTONE PASS 1: Use D7#11 only and resolve to C#m.
CAPSTONE PASS 2: Use G#7alt only and resolve to C#m.
CAPSTONE PASS 3: Choose the direct or substitute dominant by phrase function. Include one full-beat rest every four bars and close on C#m.
1. 1. D Lydian dominant shell and mode
LOST D7: play D-F#-A-C before adding G#.
LOST G#7: play G#-B#-F# before alterations.
WRONG C SPELLING: name B# over G#7 and C over D7.
SUB DOES NOT RESOLVE: make D fall to C#.
ALTERED SOUP: use one alteration and one target.
DIRECT/SUB CONFUSION: add the root beneath the shared tritone.
FORM LOSS: return to four whole-note chord targets.
- Play D Lydian dominant and G# altered in all printed routes and name every chord role.
- Resolve all D7#11 and G#7alt tension cells without losing the destination.
- Play the shared C-F# tritone in five registers and identify the root by ear.
- Perform all direct-dominant and tritone-substitute cadence pairs.
- Play all five C#-minor applied-dominant phrases and all four progression comparisons.
- Transpose the direct/substitute guide-tone relationship to C, F, A minor, and D minor.
- Perform the sixteen-bar solo and all three improvisation passes on two separate days.
Section X shifts from new scale systems to advanced integration: chromatic harmony, modulation, odd grouping, repertoire, and full-performance orchestration.

9 MODULES  |  652 TONES  |  SECTION X BEGINS
Section X shifts from new scale systems to advanced integration. Level 73 trains the ear and hand to move between tonal centers without losing voice-leading, rhythm, or phrase
identity. Some changes use a diatonic pivot chord; others use one retained pitch or a direct chromatic-mediant shift.

lines.text: COMMON-TONE AND GUIDE-TONE MODULATION, PIVOT CHORDS, CHROMATIC MEDIANTS, AND KEY-CENTER NAVIGATION

Move between tonal centers while preserving phrase identity, voice leading, rhythm, and fretboard orientation. Related-key modulations use pivot chords; distant chromatic-mediant changes retain one or more common tones and are confirmed by the destination dominant or tonic.
Pivot chord: one chord receives a Roman-numeral function in both keys.
Common-tone modulation: one pitch remains while the surrounding harmony changes.
Guide-tone modulation: inner voices move by semitone or remain common while the bass and tonic center change.
Cmaj7-Am7-D7-Gmaj7: Am7 is vi in C and ii in G.
Cmaj7-Em7-A7-Dmaj7: Em7 is iii in C and ii in D.
Cmaj7-Dm7-C7-Fmaj7: Dm7 is ii in C and vi in F.
Cmaj7 -> Emaj7: common tones E and B.
Cmaj7 -> Abmaj7: common tones C and G.
COMPLETE WRITTEN WORKOUT: 652 sounding tones before repeats.

Guitar Exercises - Section X, Level 74
Odd rhythmic groupings, cross-bar accent cycles, metric displacement, and polyrhythmic phrase control
8 MODULES  |  1168 NOTATED CONTACTS
Level 73 changed key centers while preserving phrase identity. Level 74 changes the perceived rhythmic center while preserving the meter, barline, harmony, and pulse. The player
must distinguish a grouping from a meter change, an accent from an extra attack, and a displaced phrase from a lost beat.
1. Keep the meter fixed
A 3-, 5-, or 7-note grouping can cross barlines while the
4/4 measure remains unchanged.
2. Move the accent, not the clock
The accent cycle may drift through every sixteenth slot.
The quarter-note pulse must remain steady.
3. Separate the voices
Polyrhythmic cells assign different pulses to bass and
upper voices without adding or removing time.
Core arithmetic: 16 sixteenth notes per 4/4 bar
GROUP OF 3:  LCM(16,3) = 48 slots  = 3 bars  = 16 groups
GROUP OF 5:  LCM(16,5) = 80 slots  = 5 bars  = 16 groups
GROUP OF 7:  LCM(16,7) = 112 slots = 7 bars  = 16 groups
The barline stays fixed. The accent returns to beat 1 only after the full cycle.
METRIC DISPLACEMENT:
same notes + same rhythm + different starting subdivision
POLYRHYTHM:
two simultaneous pulse organizations sharing one time span

Session protocol
Clap and count first. Next play one muted string. Then play one note. Add the pitch cell only after the accent cycle is stable. During polyrhythms, isolate each voice before combining them. A
wrong note may be repaired inside the form; a lost pulse requires a restart.
ACCENT RULE
An accent changes volume or articulation. It does not create another attack.

Guitar Exercises - Section X, Level 76
Transcription and ear-led repertoire reconstruction from audio instead of a supplied chart
SECTION X  |  EAR -> MAP -> PLAY
Level 75 began with a complete chart and trained performance orchestration. Level 76 reverses the process: the player hears an unfamiliar source, discovers its structure in layers, verifies
the result, and rebuilds a playable arrangement without depending on a prewritten chart.
1. Hear before naming
First identify repetition, pulse, and tonal center. Do not
guess chord names while the form is still unknown.
2. Reduce before decorating
Bass motion, chord quality, rhythm, and structural
melody are transcribed before fills, ornaments, and tone
details.
3. Verify by reconstruction
A transcription is accepted only when the rebuilt part
survives playback, reduced-texture testing, and a
complete performance.
The seven-pass transcription stack
PASS 1  FORM        section lengths, repeats, landmarks
PASS 2  PULSE       meter, tempo, subdivision, groove
PASS 3  BASS        roots, inversions, pedal tones
PASS 4  HARMONY     chord quality, function, extensions
PASS 5  RHYTHM      exact attack/rest/tie pattern
PASS 6  MELODY      targets, contour, articulation
PASS 7  ARRANGEMENT register, texture, dynamics, cues

Listening discipline
Use short loops. Sing or tap the answer before touching the fretboard. Write uncertainty explicitly: root=?, quality=?, rhythm=?, inversion=? A blank is better than a confident wrong answer. Slow
playback may be used after the first normal-speed pass; pitch shifting is not used until the tonal center has been estimated by ear.
SELF-STUDY SOURCE: ask a partner to perform the source cards, or record each source card once, put the page away, wait several minutes, and transcribe only from the recording.

Guitar Exercises - Section X, Level 76
The transcription workflow and uncertainty notation
DO NOT SOLVE ALL LAYERS AT ONCE
THE ORDER OF QUESTIONS PREVENTS THE FRETBOARD FROM BECOMING A GUESSING MACHINE
1. FORM
How many bars? What repeats? Where is the strongest arrival?
2. PULSE
Can I clap the beat? Is the subdivision straight, swung, triplet, or sixteenth-based?
3. TONIC
Which pitch sounds finished when the excerpt stops?
4. BASS
What is the lowest structural pitch at each change?
5. QUALITY
Major, minor, dominant, diminished, suspended, or uncertain?
6. RHYTHM
Where are the contacts, rests, ties, anticipations, and releases?
7. MELODY
Which notes are structural targets and which are approaches?
8. ARRANGEMENT
What register, density, articulation, dynamics, and cue behavior define the part?
Uncertainty marks: ? = unresolved; / = two plausible answers; ( ) = optional or ornamental; ! = verified by at least two independent clues.

Guitar Exercises - Section X, Level 78
Ear-led improvisation, anticipatory guide tones, motif prediction, and spontaneous role switching
SECTION X  |  EAR LEADS THE HAND
Level 77 connected relative hearing to immediate fretboard action. Level 78 removes the final separation between ear training and improvisation: the player hears or sings the destination
before the hand moves, predicts how a motif should continue, and changes between accompaniment and lead roles without losing the form.
1. Pre-hear
The next structural note exists in the ear before it exists
on the fretboard.
2. Predict
A motif is continued from its rhythm, contour, chord role,
and harmonic direction.
3. Switch roles
Comping and lead are two views of the same form; the
player can hand off between them on cue.
Improvisation control loop
HEAR       next chord / target / contour
SING       destination or first phrase tone
LOCATE     silent fretboard target
PLAY       target before filler
LISTEN     compare result to prediction
ANSWER     develop or contrast motif
RETURN     resume accompaniment / form

If a pre-heard target is lost, simplify the phrase to one chord tone and one rest. Do not replace prediction with fretboard searching or fill the bar with scale motion. The target and form have priority

Complete-performance improvisation and multi-system integration
SECTION X CAPSTONE  |  48-BAR PERFORMANCE
Level 79 combines the advanced systems developed across Section X into one performance problem. The player must shape a long dynamic arc, navigate changing key centers, displace
motifs rhythmically, respond to ensemble cues, switch between accompaniment and lead, and recover by ear without abandoning the form.
1. Form outranks detail
Know the bar, section, key center, and role before adding
embellishment.
2. Hear the next event
Pre-hear target, cue, or destination before the hand
commits to it.
3. Shape the whole take
Dynamics, density, register, and silence must create a
beginning, development, peak, and release.
Performance control hierarchy
1  PULSE / BAR COUNT
2  SECTION / CUE
3  KEY CENTER / HARMONY
4  ROLE: COMP OR LEAD
5  STRUCTURAL TARGET
6  REGISTER / DENSITY
7  ARTICULATION / ORNAMENT

Stop rule
If the player loses the form, stop adding lead material immediately. Reduce to roots or guide-tone shells, locate the next section landmark, and resume the intended texture only after the bar count is

The objective is not maximum technique density. A simpler performance that preserves form, cue response, harmony, and musical arc is the higher-level result.

Guitar Exercises - Section XI, Level 80
Chord melody and independent-voice control
SECTION XI START  |  10 MODULES  |  1,056 EVENTS
Level 80 begins a new specialization block: one guitarist must carry melody, harmony, bass motion, and inner voice leading at the same time. The challenge is not simply adding more notes.
Each voice must retain a distinct musical job and remain audible inside one coordinated texture.
1. Melody remains primary
The top voice must read as a melody, not as the highest
accidental chord tone.
2. Bass defines direction
Bass notes establish inversion, motion, and cadence
independently of the top line.
3. Inner voices explain harmony
Thirds and sevenths move smoothly even when the outer
voices remain fixed.
Four-voice hierarchy
VOICE 1  top melody
VOICE 2  upper guide tone
VOICE 3  lower guide tone / chord body
VOICE 4  bass / root / inversion
Priority when simplification is required:
melody -> bass -> guide tones -> extensions

Core performance rule
Play the melody alone first. Then add the bass alone. Then add inner guide tones. If the melody becomes hidden or the pulse becomes unstable, remove the least important inner voice before slowing
the tempo.
Chord melody is successful when the listener can follow the melody and the harmonic motion simultaneously.

Guitar Exercises - Section XI, Level 81
Moving inner voices, pedal tones, walking bass, passing diminished chords, and spread voicings
LEVEL 81 OF 105  |  10 MODULES  |  1,184 EVENTS
Level 81 extends chord melody from static outer-voice control into moving internal architecture. The player must now preserve a recognizable melody while bass lines walk, pedal tones remain
fixed, inner voices move chromatically, passing diminished chords connect diatonic harmony, and voicing spacing changes between compact and spread textures.
1. Preserve hierarchy
Melody and bass remain structural. Inner voices may move,
disappear, or change register without obscuring the outer
frame.
2. Movement must have a job
Walking bass, chromatic inner voices, and diminished
connectors must point toward a destination.
3. Voicing is orchestration
Drop-2 and spread voicings change register and texture;
they do not replace voice-leading logic.
Level 81 voice hierarchy
VOICE 1  melody - must remain traceable
VOICE 2  guide tone / moving inner line
VOICE 3  guide tone / pedal / chord body
VOICE 4  bass - root, inversion, or walk
Reduction order when control fails:
extensions -> fifth -> one guide tone -> full texture

Guitar Exercises - Section XI, Level 82
Walking-bass chord melody, chromatic approaches, bass substitutions, and longer solo-guitar arrangements
LEVEL 82 OF 105  |  10 MODULES  |  1,392 EVENTS
Level 82 strengthens the bass side of chord melody. The player now has to create a convincing low-register line, arrive on structural bass notes at the correct time, preserve a separate melody
above it, and re-form the harmony without interrupting the pulse.
1. Bass is a melodic voice
Roots are only the beginning. The bass can use chord
tones, scale steps, chromatic approaches, inversions, and
pedal tones.
2. Beat 1 is structural
Approach notes may be adventurous, but the destination
bass and chord must arrive cleanly at the harmonic
landmark.
3. Independence before density
Bass, melody, and chord attacks are separated rhythmically
before they are combined into full solo-guitar texture.
Bass-line construction hierarchy
1  destination root or inversion
2  chord tone on strong beat
3  diatonic connector
4  chromatic approach
5  enclosure / substitution
Reduction order when control fails:
full chord -> shell -> bass+melody -> bass only

Level 103 removes the fully written roadmap. The player must create coherent music in real time while remembering what has already happened, deciding what
should repeat, what should change, when sections should turn, and how the piece should end.

FINAL MUSICIANSHIP CAPSTONE
The Complete 105-Level Core Curriculum Examination
This is Level 105 of 105. HARD STOP. There is no Level 106 in the universal core curriculum.
The final level does not introduce a new technique, scale, chord system, or genre. It tests whether the player can integrate everything already learned into
complete musical decisions under realistic constraints.

A player may simplify any passage during the exam. Simplification is scored by whether it preserves musical function.

Standard

future study becomes specialization, repertoire, and artistic development
